It is to comply with the express terms of the National Defence Act that there must be an order in council and there must be a decision that those items, whatever the amount may be, are not immediately required. With respect to commercial transactions involving property that is not that of the government, the matter is governed by the

Export and Import Permits Act, which authorizes the Minister of Trade and Commerce to issue export permits, and those matters are dealt with in conformity with the terms of those two statutes in question.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED INVITATION TO EXPRESS VIEWS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED INVITATION TO EXPRESS VIEWS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Will the minister, either now or in his address later this afternoon, comment on the report that Britain and Russia have invited the views of ten other countries, including Canada, on ways of ensuring the fulfilment of the Viet Nam armistice agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED INVITATION TO EXPRESS VIEWS
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of this question and I think probably it would be better if I dealt with it now. The reply is as follows.
In its fourth interim report the international supervisory commission in Viet Nam pointed out that the co-operation being extended by the parties to the commission was unsatisfactory. The commission asked the co-chairmen to consider this problem and the United Kingdom and Soviet foreign ministers, the two co-chairmen under the Geneva conference arrangement, have requested the views of the members of the Geneva conference and the commission powers on this somewhat difficult problem. So far as I know the Chinese reply is the first one to be made to the co-chairmen. I would expect that the co-chairmen would wish to wait until they had received replies from other governments before trying to decide what would be the right course of action to take in the circumstances.
Canada, of course, is not a member of the Geneva conference on Indo-China, but was invited at the end of it to serve on the international supervisory commissions together with India and Poland. Our position is therefore somewhat different from that of the members of the Geneva conference, but we are at the moment considering the views that we should send on this matter in reply to the letter from the co-chairmen. There may be an opportunity later in the session or before the committee on external affairs to make those views public.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It has been a well known rule of the department not to answer questions on current wheat transactions. My hon. friend could ask me today how many bushels we have sold to Poland, and tomorrow how many bushels we have sold to the United Kingdom, and following that how much to Germany, thus telling our competitors our exact position in every market, which obviously would destroy our ability to sell wheat.

Mr. Speaker, on January 25 the hon. member for York South, whose absence because of illness I am sure we all regret, asked the following questions:
Has the Department of National Defence ever ordered the demolition of the shacks on its property at Long Branch, Toronto? If so, have these orders been carried out? If not, why not, and what use is now being made of these shacks?
I take it that the hon. member was referring to certain wartime buildings on the Long Branch rifle range property still being used as civilian emergency housing by the city of Toronto.
According to our records, the Department of National Defence has had no jurisdiction over these buildings since they were declared surplus in 1946-47, at which time the crown assets allocation committee allocated them to the department of reconstruction and supply to be made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for emergency shelter.
I am informed that shortly after that date the city of Toronto by arrangement with Central Mortgage and Housing took over the buildings, and I am further informed that the city of Toronto still holds them. In any event these buildings have not been under the jurisdiction or control of the Department of National Defence for almost 10 years; consequently the department has not ordered their demolition, nor has it in fact any right to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion will give the house an opportunity to discuss international affairs, and it gives me the privilege of introducing that discussion. I realize that in the time I can appropriately take in a debate of this kind there will be many important questions in international affairs with which I will not be able to deal. I hope, however, that when the time comes for me to close the discussion I will be able to answer questions that may be raised subsequently and which I have not dealt with in my opening statement.
One subject I will not touch on in this speech, because I attempted to deal with it last week in the debate on the address, is Middle East policy. If any questions are raised in this debate dealing with the policy that should be followed in that area in the
External Affairs
preservation of peace-and, after all, that is the thing that matters-or in respect of the administration of that policy, I would hope to deal with them again when I wind up the debate.
I will also not be able, in this discussion, to touch on the work of the United Nations or more particularly the work of the recent United Nations assembly. I hope there will be an opportunity before long for my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), to deal with the work of that assembly to which, if I may say so, he made such a distinguished and constructive contribution.
I would also have liked to report in some detail, and I hope to do so as soon as possible when the opportunity presents itself, either here or in the committee on external affairs, on the recent ministerial meeting of the Colombo plan countries at Singapore. It was a most successful and inspiring meeting, a meeting of especial significance because it was held in a colony now on the threshold of self-government, a secure freedom and a selfgovernment achieved by evolution which would have been impossible under a communist form of government, which makes some of the allegations of recent communist travellers in that part of the world sound pretty ridiculous.
After that conference in Singapore I had the privilege of seeing the Colombo plan in action in India and in Pakistan, where my colleagues and myself were received by the governments of those two countries with very great kindness and were given a very sincere welcome.
After this opportunity of seeing it in action I returned more convinced than ever of the value of the Colombo plan based on friendly co-operation without political pressure and justified now by performance. Promises are no longer needed for that purpose. It will have been noticed by the house that the government intends to recommend to parliament a substantial increase this year in our contribution to the Colombo plan, namely an increase of almost 33J per cent. That increase will not quite meet the figure advocated last year by my friend the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who had urged us to double our contribution, but it is a substantial increase and I hope it will be voted by parliament.
I should also, Mr. Speaker, say at least a word about the work of the armistice commissions in Indo-China, which was referred to earlier in the sitting this afternoon. In that area of the world Canadians continue to make an important contribution to peace

External Affairs
through their work with these commissions. Our men-there are some 170 of them in that area, mostly from the Department of National Defence, members of the armed forces-have discharged their extremely difficult and trying duties with great credit to themselves and to their country. In one of the countries there, namely Cambodia, we have reached the winding-up stage of the commission, and we have been able to reduce the strength of that commission. Elections have been held in that country, and as a result the commission and its members can leave Cambodia with the satisfaction which they must feel at the stability which has been achieved in a country so recently a victim of war.
In Laos, one of the other countries, the situation is not so good. Elections have also been held there, but the communist Pathet Lao forces, which are grouped in the northern provinces of that country, have refused to accept the Laotian government or the authority of that government and to take part in the election. Hence no reduction there has been found possible either in the numbers of the commission or in its activities up to the present time.
So far as Viet Nam is concerned-and that is probably the most important of the three countries-the military phases of the armistice work have been completed and with little disturbance. I think the commission deserves a good deal of credit for that result. The political aspects, however, present a less satisfactory picture. Little progress has been made in that country toward the national elections visualized by the Geneva conference, and which are scheduled to take place in July of this year. If they do not take place it is hard to say what effect that failure will have on our obligations in the commission.
This work in Indo-China is arduous and difficult, as I have said, and it imposes a heavy burden on the armed forces of our country and upon the Department of External Affairs. We are most anxious to complete it at the earliest possible date. Nevertheless we shall not abandon that work so long as we are convinced that it is making an important contribution to peace.
I should also, Mr. Speaker, say a word about a problem which is very much in our mind these days, namely that of the legal recognition of the communist Chinese government in Peking. One of the most difficult questions which face this country and many other countries is that of determining our relations with the two rival and bitterly hostile governments of China. It is not as simple an issue to decide as some seem to
FMr. Pearson.]
think. There is more than one factor to take into account before any decisions can wisely be taken. Such a decision requires a careful balancing of many national and international factors, moral, political and economic.
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker-indeed, last summer-I expressed the view that we should have another look at this question in the light of the cessation of hostilities in Korea and in Indo-China, in the light of the situation in and around the Formosa straits and in the light of the recent policy of the Peking government in so far as it is possible to determine it. We have made this reexamination and we feel that the careful policy we have been following, and are still following, has been the right one; rejecting on the one hand immediate diplomatic recognition but rejecting on the other hand the view that a communist regime in Peking can never be recognized as the government of China.
The arguments for and against recognition of this government have more than once been discussed, and in detail, in this house, and I do not intend to repeat them at this time. I wish merely to state as briefly as possible the considerations which determine our policy as a government in this matter.
The first consideration is the interest of our country, remembering that the paramount interest of us all is international peace and security. In addition, we are obliged to give consideration to the interests and views of our friends and allies, some of whom are even more directly involved than are we in the consequences of diplomatic recognition. It is also important, Mr. Speaker, not to confuse recognition with approval. There are, of course, moral considerations involved and, in the case of a ruthless communist regime, these considerations inevitably must have a bearing on our attitude. But the decision remains predominantly a political one to be taken on the basis of enlightened self-interest, as in many other cases where we have recognized totalitarian regimes.
It should not, however, be assumed that Canadian recognition of the Peking government-even if it were to be granted at some time in the future-would extend to the island of Formosa. As we see it, the legal status of Formosa is still undecided and no step taken vis-a-vis the communist regime should prejudice that issue. In particular, we would not be a party to any action which handed over the people or the government on Formosa, against their will, to any mainland government, let alone to a communist Chinese government.
We condemn the cruelties and tyrannies of the Peking regime, and we continue to hope

that the Chinese people will one day be governed by a more enlightened government of their own choice.
But, Mr. Speaker, we must accept the fact of communist control of mainland China. That is one thing we cannot fail to recognize, with the corollary that in certain circumstances and in our own interests we may be obliged to deal-as we already have been obliged to do-at Geneva and elsewhere with that government in respect of certain problems which cannot be solved without it. Nor should we, I suggest, base our policy on the likelihood of the nationalist government of Chiang Kai-shek returning to power on the mainland. Furthermore, the anomaly of that government representing China at the United Nations, with a veto that can block any action desired by 52 other members, is becoming increasingly apparent. I believe also that we should accept no commitment to intervene on behalf of the nationalist government in the struggle for the Chinese offshore islands. Our view on this matter has already been made clear in this house, outside this house and in the United States.
As for Formosa, the only commitment-and this also has been stated in the house- we have is that which might arise out of our obligations under the charter of the United Nations. So far as diplomatic recognition is concerned, we should from time to time review the position in the light of conditions; of our own interests and of the views of our friends and allies. However, I believe we should not get ourselves into such an inflexible position that a change in policy, if it were considered to be wise and necessary, could be brought about only with maximum difficulty.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express one further thought on this subject. We are all concerned, and rightly so, that the utmost in good judgment be applied to this complicated and controversial problem of legal recognition. As I see it, however, we must not let it distract us so much that we ignore the longer term issues which are raised by communist China's emergence as a new and powerful force in the world. The consolidation and growth of Chinese power under communist rule which is now taking place may be historically as important an event as the Russian revolution of 1917. The implications for us in China's determined drive to achieve military and industrial might and a position as a world power may be as far reaching as similar developments which have taken place in Russia. Indeed, one day in the future these two revolutionary forces may clash. It may now seem to us to be of great importance to recognize or not to recognize
External Affairs
the communist regime in Peking. It is of far greater importance to recognize that a revolution of cataclysmic force has taken place in China as a fateful part of the emergence of a modern awakened Asia. [DOT]
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like for a few moments to make a report, if I may call it that-and I am afraid it will not be a very adequate one because of considerations of time-on my recent visit to the Soviet union. You will remember that this visit, and it was an encouraging thought for me, was made with the approval of all parties in this House of Commons. I am quite aware of the fact, as I have said before, that one can acquire in a brief official visit only impressions. Those impressions can be misleading, but they can be valuable as a check on studies that have already been made, and as a check on the experiences of others. They can also be valuable if your visit brings you into contact, as mine did, with the top rulers of the country. Therefore it may be that the impressions I brought back, though I give them without any feeling of certainty or dogmatism, may be of some value.
So far as the people of this powerful country are concerned, they showed us a hospitality, a kindness and courtesy which I have great pleasure in acknowledging. This, of course, reflected the traditional hospitality and kindness of the Russian people, and it has little, if anything, to do with their form of government. They seemed, in so far as we were able to determine it, to have a pride in the achievements of their state. They seemed to have a fear of war, and there is no reason why the people of that country should not have a fear of war. No other people in the world have suffered more from war than they have. But they also seem to have an ignorance of the world outside which is frightening indeed.
One gets the impression also that there has been a relaxation of tension inside the country. The long-range importance of that may be considerable. It is true that that kind of relaxation can be turned on and off easily by the governing group, even by an editorial in Pravda. It would be unwise, therefore, to draw any far-reaching conclusions from such a development. I had an abiding impression when I left of great strength, great power, great richness, a state of collective power and collective riches alongside individual deprivations. But I think it is correct to say that the latter is decreasing, and bread and circuses are increasing. I think it is also right to say that the former, the collective power, is also increasing. We would be making a great mistake if we underrated that development.

External Affairs
That country, Mr. Speaker, is harnessing education and science, propaganda and power to communist imperialism.
The Russian regime, which embodies this communist imperialism, is achieving a strength, a solidity, a dynamism that is impressive-indeed, it is frightening. Their plans to increase this are even more impressive. Let us not deceive ourselves, if anyone still does, by thinking that they are a beaten, lifeless people in an ox-cart civilization. It is true that many of the comforts to which we are accustomed are missing, but this does not seem to either weaken or worry them. To them plumbing is not as important as plutonium; ease is not as important as engineering; man is only material for management. There is no obvious sign, Mr. Speaker, that they resent these things. Those who do, no doubt, are in jail or in concentration camps.
So far as the government of the country is concerned, as the house knows, one man has now been succeeded by a group. Of that group, two men seem to be in the ascendancy, two men who are in startling contrast to each other in so many ways but who seem to work very closely together indeed. These two men in the conversations I had with them profess, and I underline the word "profess" because it has sometimes been left out of the reports which have been previously ascribed to me on this matter, to have no other desire than peace and further relaxation of tension.
Indeed on this trip, Mr. Speaker, we heard much talk about peace. It was the first Russian word I learned, and it was the last one I heard as we took off from the Crimean airport. This peace talk, this peace cry, may well be genuine when it is uttered by the people, but that is not important unless it can influence the policies of the leaders of the people and there is not so much evidence of that. Mr. Khrushchev's idea of peace, and he made no secret about it when he talked with me, is illustrated by his determination to break up NATO as an aggressive organization, so he claimed, aimed at Russia and therefore a threat to peace. I, of course, argued with him long and loudly on this matter, but I have some doubt whether I made very much impression.
I feel, however, that he wishes to break up NATO primarily because, in his professed view, it is an agency of aggressive United States policy. The United States is the culprit. Similarly with Germany; he fears it I believe chiefly as a member of NATO and as such, in his view, an agent of the United States. He was not interested in my argument that a Germany armed and outside NATO might be a far greater danger to the

Soviet union than a Germany that was one of 15 countries, with limited arms and under collective control inside NATO. Mr. Khrushchev also seemed worried that the Russian initiative, as he would put it, in relaxing tension might be interpreted in the west as a sign of weakness or even of crisis at home. He frankly admitted they were having difficulties, especially in agricultural production, but he became almost violent in denying any weakness or any crisis.
He went on to assure me that the Soviet union was never stronger, and if anyone dared to begin a war with them the Russians would finish it. He talks with an easy assurance on these matters that amounts almost to arrogance. My own view for what it is worth is that the leaders of the Soviet union do want what I call a peaceful interlude, and for a variety of reasons. Among others, as Mr. Khrushchev has candidly admitted, in a more peaceful atmosphere the democracies-he thinks their people are soft and undisciplined, that freedom is licence and will be their undoing-will not accept the sacrifices that prolonged defence preparations involve and will fall apart in their coalitions, especially in NATO.
Communists, he assured me, could stand up to effort and sacrifice far better than we could. They were tougher and more patient, and therefore communism would be superior to capitalism in peaceful but competitive coexistence. He was supremely confident, and expressed that confidence on a good many occasions, that communism will conquer in this kind of competition.
Our hosts, Mr. Speaker, expressed a very high regard for Canada. Those expressions may have been more calculated than spontaneous; nevertheless I think they have a real respect for our country, not only because of our efforts and sacrifices in war, but also because we have tried to be objective and internationally useful in peace and are nobody's tool. They are, of course, pretty obvious in their efforts to distinguish us and ultimately detach us from our southern neighbour, and their insistence that we have a northern neighbour as well was not as reassuring, at least to me, as they tried to make it sound. But when I emphasized, as I did, the bonds of friendship between the United States and Canada, or tried to say a good word for the United States, they at least listened politely. Similarly when we opposed certain of their suggestions, as we had to do, that the trade treaty which we were discussing should be concluded at once in Moscow, or that certain phrases or ideas should be included in the communique which

we thought might be misinterpreted in Canada-when we took that position of opposition they took it in good part and did not press us too hard.
I think the visit was worth while for us who were privileged to undertake it. Apart from any concrete advantages that may possibly arise out of it in the way of trade, or in the way of scientific and technical exchanges, or in getting information out of Russia in regard to relatives of Canadians, in addition to those concrete advantages if they should come about I think as the result of a visit of this kind one is in a better position to appreciate and understand the sources of soviet power and the nature of soviet policy.
Whatever was gained in this respect was accomplished, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, without misleading them as to the views and policies of Canada and her friends. Indeed, having heard from Mr. Khrushchev soviet views stated with great force and with great frankness, I was encouraged to reply in kind. They may not, as I have said, have made much of an impression on him or on his colleagues; but at least they know, I hope, a little more about our views; that the west, in the United Nations or in NATO, is not and will not become aggressive or warmongering and is as vitally concerned, as they told me they were, with peace, security and the removal of causes of war. I hope they realize also that I was right when I said we were not going to throw away NATO merely because of doses, large or small, of the Geneva spirit.
Mention of the Geneva spirit brings me to the question, where are we today in respect of the relaxation of tension which we hoped had been initiated at the Geneva conference last July, and which we hoped would continue and indeed would show concrete results in policy. Hon. members will recall the feeling of optimism that was developed at the summit meeting, as it is now called, at Geneva last summer. It may well be that hopes at that time were too high and that thinking was too wishful. I remember, along with others, taking that view in this house in the discussion we had on July 23 last year. At that time I, along with a good many others, felt that the real test of the reality and importance of the Geneva spirit was to be the foreign ministers' meeting which was called for November in an effort to achieve some of the objectives of the summit meeting.
We now know that the result of that November meeting was almost 100 per cent negative. We learned at that time that soviet words differed from soviet deeds, and that soviet tactics were not the same as soviet policy. As hon. members will recall, as a result of that foreign ministers' meeting in 67509-46
External Affairs
Geneva in November, not a single basic objective of soviet policy was changed.
What are those objectives? I believe myself, Mr. Speaker, that the fundamental objective of soviet policy, the long-range one, is security for the Soviet union and the triumph of communist ideology in a world of communist states controlled and dominated by Moscow, I believe this objective remains unaffected either by relaxation or by increases of tension. The cold war in that sense goes on, and I suggest it is misleading to think of the cold war in any other terms.
This was very well put in an editorial in The Economist magazine last November, which reads:
"Cold war" is an even more misleading phrase than most of the monosyllabic slogans that headline writers love. It is commonly identified with such rudeness and crudeness as the Russians practised until lately. For those who make this over-simple identification, the "cold war" presumably ended when Vishinsky's diatribes gave place to Mr. Khrushchev's waggery, . . . "Cold war" in that sense need not now return, and it probably will not . . . But the phrase "cold war" was originally coined with reference not to a form of etiquette but to a policy-the policy of "struggle", to borrow a communist keyword. This "struggle" is basically a contest for power over men's minds, a political contest in which economic and military pressures are auxiliary. The "cold war" in this deeper sense never ended, and can never end while the communist rulers cling to their aim of worldwide victory. All that can change is the tactics employed, both by them and by the nations that are ready to defend their liberty.
These, Mr. Speaker, are very wise words indeed. But tactics, even on this interpretation of soviet policy, have changed, and in one sense at least I think the change of tactics has effected a change of strategy, and in a sense that is very important indeed.
I believe myself, and I share that belief, of course, with many others, that the deterrent effect of the hydrogen bomb is now recognized in Moscow. It is now admitted there as in other places that hydrogen warfare means universal destruction, and it is now accepted in Moscow, as in other places, that a balance of terror has been achieved. No one, however, can take much comfort out of it as a solid foundation of peace.
I think, as I said a few moments ago, that the soviet leaders do want peace in the sense that they do not want atomic warfare, and that they will not deliberately provoke or risk that kind of war with the certainty of mutual destruction. Yet I add that in my view their policy is still conflict short of war that is what they mean, surely, by competitive coexistence; not friendly cooperation.
It is always wise, Mr. Speaker, to go to the soviet leaders' own words to get inside their

is one of manoeuvre and contact, of trying everything that may help their cause; of smiles and scowls, of kicks and carrots. These tactics may be more dangerous and difficult to deal with than any ever employed by Stalin. They are certainly more complex. But at any rate, in the long run, they may offer some possibilities for negotiation and settlement. To meet them and to bring about that negotiation and settlement to which we would all give first place in our efforts, requires flexibility and imagination on our part. As "our" refers to a coalition of free states, with a cherished freedom even to differ, this is going to be difficult to combine with unity of purpose and co-ordination of methods.
We must, then, develop an imaginative yet realistic diplomacy, one based on a clear and unclouded understanding of the intentions and methods of the Soviet union and its satellites and of their strengths and weaknesses; one based also on a staunch adherence to our own policies and principles.
There is now less reason for complacency on our part than ever, for the threat to the institutions and the society of the free world remains as strong as ever. There is, however, no reason for despair merely because Mr. Molotov said "Nyet" at Geneva and because Mr. Bulganin and Mr. Khrushchev continue to level harsh and unfounded accusations at the western powers, mixed with honeyed words and offers of peace pacts. The latest of these offers was made the other day to the government of the United States through a message from Mr. Bulganin to President Eisenhower. I feel that I am voicing the impressions of most members of this house, though I know I should speak only for myself, when I say that I have read with admiration and respect the reply of the President of the United States to that offer. It was constructive, not negative, and it was the sort of attitude that in a matter of this kind I am sure this government would be happy to support.
I have already mentioned the feeling of confidence and self-assurance of the Soviet leaders. If on our part we can show strength, steadiness and unity-a strength which is more than military, a steadiness which is not indifference and a unity which is based on common ideals and which requires careful and continuous fostering-we shall prove the communists wrong in their assurance that the future belongs to them.
If we do not, we shall have only ourselves to blame.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hate to interrupt the hon. member, but at the time that statement appeared in the press I denied I had said that. I also mentioned the matter this afternoon. The radio recording of the interview will show quite conclusively that the word "professed", which is a very important one, was put in that statement.

I can understand the applause with which that statement is received. As a matter of fact, if my hon. friend says he denied the statement the publicity given to the denial never caught up with the publicity given to the words that he allegedly said.
It never does.
Oh, oh.

We listened with a good deal of composure when my hon. friend was speaking. Surely we are not going to depart from the attitude adopted in the past of endeavouring to discuss these issues in a manner befitting their seriousness. Today, sir, we have the minister again facing reality, if at any time the red carpet of welcome caused any distortion in objectivity during the course of his visit. The big problem the free nations of the world have to face is this: Is the change since the Geneva conference a new look? Is it reality or is it a mirage? Is it a change in manner or a change in matter? That to me represents in summary the problem that faces us today.
The minister referred particularly to the words of Khrushchev in connection with the shrimp whistling, and in listening to the minister I thought of history itself. A reading of recent history shows that on every occasion that the U.S.S.R. has ceased to be openly aggressive time was being bought for a purpose favourable to the U.S.S.R. I go back to 1921 to a book by Mikkail Frunske which is still standard in all military academies. In it he said that the general purpose and aim

of the policies of the U.S.S.R. are that a death struggle with the western democracies is inevitable. In 1917, after the treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the foreign minister of the U.S.S.R. said: "We entered into that agreement. We never intended to keep it. We were simply buying time for a breathing spell."
The minister mentioned one of the latest actions on the part of the U.S.S.R., the offer of a 20-year treaty of friendship pact with the United States, a simple scheme designed to drive a wedge between the United Kingdom and the commonwealth on the one hand and the United States on the other. The friendly letter received by President Eisenhower from the communist leader is not in keeping with the unfriendly and provocative actions of the U.S.S.R. during recent weeks. In particular I refer to the speeches delivered by the communist leaders during their recent trip to India and eastern Asia.
The minister has stated that what is needed today is a realization of the unity of the free nations and an intensification of that unity. He mentioned the United States. I intended to quote an editorial from Sunday's New York Times, I believe, where, dealing with the present visit of Sir Anthony Eden to the President of the United States the New York Times makes it perfectly clear that there will be no freedom, no security, no salvation from the onrush of communism if at any time the United Kingdom and the commonwealth and the United States follow different courses of action or cease to be united in their common crusade.
This is not the first time that the U.S.S.R. has offered a non-aggression pact such as it offers the United States. It did the same in the Balkan states. It did the same with Finland. One thing I thought the minister might mention was the visit to Ottawa next Monday of Sir Anthony Eden who will be given a reception in our country, as he is receiving today in the United States, a reception in keeping with the magnificent contribution he and those associated with him are making to the preservation of world peace today.
The minister revealed some of his impressions, and I think that we in the various parties in the house who suggested that he should visit the U.S.S.R. have reason to be pleased that he did and that he has brought back to us that reaction which only the intimacy of personal intercourse can bring about. I am going to suggest, having regard to the experience some of us had last summer in visiting the NATO representatives of other countries and also having regard to the experience of the minister himself, that we in
External Affairs
Canada should follow somewhat the same system followed by the congress of the United States, to make opportunities available for members of the Canadian Senate and House of Commons to visit the U.S.S.R. and there learn something at first hand of the situation in that country and of the attitude taken by the U.S.S.R.
To bring together representatives produces results. The agriculturists from the U.S.S.R., who recently visited North America and on occasion received a welcome not in keeping with our democratic way of life, had nothing adverse to say about our countries in their report on their return to Russia. Indeed, there is the highest commendation of the manner in which we discharge our responsibilities to our agricultural economy. While the U.S.S.R. originally made the offer suggesting exchanges in a manner that is not in keeping with our parliamentary way of invitation, I think that in the interests of all the government of this country through you, Your Honour, should make available in clear-cut terms an invitation to the U.S.S.R. to send representatives to our country.
I know that there has been ridicule of such visits._ There were some who said: What are we going to do when we go to visit the NATO parliamentary association? I can say that those who were there came back with a new realization of the need of maintaining and expanding NATO. They came back with a new appreciation of world events in general. They sat in conference with representatives of 14 other NATO nations, and we saw there on two occasions an answer to those who say that there is a finality in history. One of the most impressive was at the NATO parliamentary conference. France demanded that the nations represented at that conference should be listed on the basis of the French names of their countries, thereby placing Germany or Allemagne in the position of being No. 1. Here I wish to pay tribute to the president of that organization, Senator Robertson of our own country, whose contribution in bringing the parliamentarians together is worthy of commendation from all of us. Imagine this. After two world wars, after all the antipathies and animosities of a thousand years, in a few short months after the inclusion of West Germany in the NATO organization, the representatives from France, in compassion and in a desire to bind the wounds of war and abate the hatreds of generations, made that request. Who would have believed that possible five years ago or even three years ago?
I saw something else. It was something that recalled to memory where we were in West Germany, in that area of Alsace-Lorraine which for generations has been the

External Affairs
way of marching armies. The representative forces of the Canadian army put on that magnificent drama, as I call it, the retreat ceremony. Taking part were representatives of the Royal 22nd regiment and two other Canadian regiments. Their respective bands performed at the ceremony. At the conclusion of that retreat ceremony "God save the Queen" was played, then "The Marseillaise," and the officers came to the salute. Then the German national anthem was played and the Canadian officers followed suit. They came to the salute in an area where there are graves that will be unforgotten for all generations. They came to the salute, thus indicating that history is not finality and that as the pages turn, changes take place.
I went into East Germany. I visited West Germany. I saw West Berlin and I am going to make just passing reference to what I saw because the minister stated that the mass of propaganda of the U.S.S.R. is designed to control the hearts and the minds of men. As you go into Berlin

that island of freedom, to use the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on one occasion -you find that West Berlin is lit up. East Berlin is dark with the exception of one street, the show street, Stalin Allee, where live in fear the dictators of communism. You met the mayor and the people. They stood there as the bulwarks of freedom. They could be overrun at any time but they have stood their ground. Then you go to East Berlin. I had no idea of the propaganda that goes on. Wherever a person goes he is facing a propaganda message. The walls of all the buildings have on them messages such as these: We demand the outlawing of all atomic weapons; fight in resistance to the Paris treaties; protect the accomplishments of the people; fight for the rebuilding of Germany as a peace-loving democratic state; workers in city and country be prepared to arm for the defence of our homeland; all Germans with their feet under the same table. These slogans are the kind that have been designed to influence the thinking of the people. They ask for unification. The mayor of West Berlin, Herr Otto Suhr, stated that unless there is unification under a system of free elections there can never be peace in Europe. The U.S.S.R. promises hopefully that there will be unification and goes its way raising East Germany to a position of equality under the Warsaw pact, demanding at all times that Canada, Great Britain, the United States and the other nations that have representatives in West Berlin shall recognize the authority of that government by allowing that government to sign the necessary authority for them to go into East Germany.

I want to say this, Mr. Speaker, before I come to controversial things. One of the most impressive things that faces a Canadian as he goes through Europe and visits the Canadian embassies is the high quality of the Canadian representatives there. Without separating him from the rest, I mention particularly Mr. Keith, the head of the military mission in West Germany. It was obvious that he was a man who enjoyed the right of entry at any time to any of the representatives of the other countries, not only because of his official position but also because of his unusual ability and his unusual insight into external affairs.
Having said that, I come to something else. When you speak to people in East Berlin, you find that they would like to be joined together. You see the difference in economic conditions. I say through you, sir, to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that butter prices there are interesting. In West Berlin butter is 72 cents a pound and in East Berlin it is $4.80 a pound. One reason for that situation is the different standard with regard to currency. But more particularly the reason is this. Under communism agriculture has been destroyed. My hon. friend stated that the U.S.S.R. wants to pick off the cream, in effect, under any system of reorganization or system of unification. That is obvious in East Germany. There the U.S.S.R. picks off the top of everything that the farmer grows. The result is a failure in agriculture that is apparent on every hand. That is one of the reasons that during the next five years the U.S.S.R., under its new agricultural policy, intends to put into crop some 75 million acres more than have previously been planted.
What is the attitude of the U.S.S.R.? Is it desirous of peace? The events of the past give no such indication. The minister stated that those high in authority in the U.S.S.R. know the danger today of the hydrogen bomb. I believe that is so. As a matter of fact, the hydrogen bomb has created equality in military preparedness today and, in my opinion, in large measure accounts for the tremendous change in objective on the part of the U.S.S.R. since the summit conference in the summer of 1955. They realize today that they are not going to overrun the world by force and they now resort to this new plan of economic infiltration, the handing out of promises, the dangling of promises before the eyes of peoples less highly developed economically than are we. They offer to India several hundreds of millions of dollars for dams, steel mills and the like; to Egypt one-half a billion dollars for the building of a dam. To other countries there have been promises of a similar nature.

My hon. friend says that Canada has increased her contribution to the Colombo plan. It is true that she has increased her contribution but it is a small increase having regard to the change in strategy on the part of the U.S.S.R. I refer to this change from reliance on the force of arms to reliance on the power of economic infiltration and the dangling of promises. As a matter of fact, having regard to the five-year plan that was recently enunciated by the U.S.S.R., I think that a form of economic blackmail is to be the policy of the U.S.S.R. during the next five years. They will make promises. They are buying surplus products from Burma. They are extending economic assistance to various countries. They do not intend to go to war, that is to hot war. They realize the fabulous dangers that they face. Now, they are proceeding on what they call a five-year plan designed, to use the words of Molotov, to change over as painlessly as possible to communism in the world. In other words, as Khrushchev once said, the danger is capitalism, and that sums up the plan today.
There is this economic change. Steel production and coal production are being expanded; hydro power is being doubled and heavy industry is being expanded as never before. They have nothing to worry about so far as the costs of production are concerned because they have a police state. They can maintain whatever level of wages they choose. This new policy has all the appearance of a vast economic war which we in the industrial nations still face as a potential danger. We in the agricultural nations, faced with this expansion in agricultural development, will find that the competition we have today will be regarded as nothing beside that which we will face in the future.
As a result of this economic plan on a large scale the western world today meets a challenge from the U.S.S.R. in this new policy of maintaining peace. Russia is putting the western nations in a challenging position by failing to go to war, by fomenting trouble, by extending economic aid, by forcing them to compete with the promises of economic aid given by the U.S.S.R., thereby endangering ourselves if we endeavour to equal in reality the promises of the U.S.S.R. Each of these countries, Poland, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Rumania and Bulgaria, united the other day under the Warsaw pact agreement, is building vast economic developments so they will be in a position to challenge the economic magnitude of the United States, Britain and the other countries of the commonwealth and the free nations. In other words, today the free nations are going through a form of international brainwashing.

Some time ago a Pole was describing the brainwashing through which he had gone. He said it consisted of sweet talk accompanied by promises of concessions. Day after day different concessions are promised until finallj the individual becomes a neurotic wreck Postponing a performance always ends in uncertainties, and the dangling of hope destroys the power of the individual to resist Is that what the U.S.S.R. is trying to dc today by promises to Asia and to Africa, as well as to the other parts of the world? Is she trying, by handing out hopeless promises, to destroy the resistance of these nations whc today find themselves economically in a position of semi-destitution, in some cases ol almost complete destitution?
It is for that reason that more than ever ] should like to see the NATO nations give greater attention to article 2 of the NATO agreement. In this way the free nations might join in multilateral trade and remove many of those tariffs that are unjust, unfair and unjustifiable in the world in which we live, to the end that the NATO nations and other free nations will be able to take their stand against this economic new look which endeavours to do what the military fierce look was not able to achieve. Indeed, in East Germany I noticed that seven or eight months of smiling had achieved more for the U.S.S.R. than seven or eight years of snarling. In other words, this new scheme shows a flexibility of policy under the present leaders that Stalin never achieved or never tried to achieve.
Now, having dealt with these generalities, I come to various more specific issues. I was interested in what the minister had to say about the recognition of communist China. A few months ago, on August 25, he made a speech in Vancouver in which he dealt with the question of recognition. He said:
I mention these matters not to indicate that we are rushing into-or should rush into-any change of policy in this matter of diplomatic recognition, in a way that would cause bitter controversy at home and with certain friendly nations. I am suggesting, however, that the time is coming-and soon-when we should have another and searching look at the problem; that we should consider it also with those friendly governments with whom we like to act-and whenever possible should act together on matters of international importance.
Well, sir, out of this searching look has come the general statement on the part of the minister today. Strangely enough only recently he was giving advice to the United States in an article in Look magazine. Apparently on January 10 he advised the United States somewhat differently, at least that is

he way the people of the United States read t. Paragraph 4 of his advice reads:
We should recognize the fact that the Peiping [overnment and not Chiang Kai-shek is in control if continental China and likely to remain so; that here are basic problems to be settled in the Far Cast which cannot be settled without the participa-ion and agreement of that government. We can legotiate with Peiping when necessary and desir-tble without implying approval of that regime or vithout weakening our opposition to communism.

What he says today represents the ittitude taken by the Leader of the Opposition Mr. Drew) and this party. We do not say ve will never consent to recognition of com-nunist China. Certainly, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) was not so sure about recognition. He did not have the same views in November ;hat the minister had when he spoke in Van-:ouver and flew that kite to the women's association out there.
The Minister of Fisheries had his experi-ince when he was actually channelled into places to which he did not want to go. He was channelled into China. In his interview >n November 11 he finally ended up in this way:
Mr. Sinclair said the United Nations had laid lown certain standards for peace-loving nations and it might be questioned if communist China met these standards. It had played a "cat-and-mouse game'' in the release of 47 missionaries recently, failing to let them go in a group and leaving those waiting to receive them at Hong Kong uncertain of time of arrival.
Such acts made it difficult for some to see they were quite ready for admission to the United Nations.
As far as recognition is concerned, while some may say it is different from admission ;o the United Nations, it indeed has very nuch the same results. The minister said ;here is one thing in the recognition of China ;hat we should take into consideration, and ;hat is, what is best for Canada? I am asking lim, to use his own words, the words he used to the Women's Canadian Club in Vancouver: Was our own national advantage me of those things that were to be considered,
EMr. Diefenbaker.]
and if there were recognition would we get paid for the Ming Sung shipping deal? Was that one of the things? In the minister's enunciation of policy today with respect to recognition he adopted the point of view which we expressed on more than one occasion, and on one occasion in particular, paraphrasing those immortal words of the late Mackenzie King: "not necessarily recognition, but recognition if necessary".
We now come to one problem that I am surprised the minister stayed away from. While he did give a casual examination to the Middle East situation the other day, I believe, Mr. Speaker, the events of the last few days and the bungling answers of the government in regard to the shipment of Harvard aircraft to Egypt have resulted in an understandable predilection against discussing this matter any further. I can quite understand that. What are those events? Well, Mr. Speaker, read Hansard if you would like to see the greatest collection of jarring, irreconcilable answers made by different ministers at different times or by the same minister at different times. It is one of the most peculiar incidents that have happened in this parliament. It is very unusual. I hold in my hand copies of Hansard and I intend to refer to them in a general way. I start first with the inexcusable attitude of this government toward parliament. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-he is not in his seat at the moment-spoke at a dinner given in his honour and in honour of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and both were entitled to all honour. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce decided to give the people assembled there a lesson in parliamentary procedure. He prefaced his remarks by saying: "I am a House of Commons man". Well, Mr. Speaker, that indeed will arouse tremendous interest in the mind of Sir Winston Churchill who described himself in that way on one occasion.
I ask the Prime Minister, through you, sir, what is the reason for all this evasive bungling that has been going on since this matter was first brought up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) on January 11? I am not going to read the record in detail, but it is a record that I doubt whether the Prime Minister, with all his masterful legal skill, could bring into anything but disorder. I ask this question because if they did not have anything to hide, one wonders, why all the hiding. If there was not something they did not want to reveal, why all the explanation?
On January 11 the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked the Secretary of State

for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) the following question, as reported at page 9 of Hansard:
Have any aircraft been shipped from Canada to Egypt recently or are there any orders on hand for the export of such aircraft?
After a few preliminary words, the minister said:
I would have to make inquiries of the Department of Trade and Commerce as well as my own department. However, I believe I can say at once that I know of no shipments of Canadian aircraft to Egypt or of any orders for such shipments.
It is strange. Today the Prime Minister said that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was consulted. First they said they did not know anything, and I am not blaming him. The subject of the question sat there. Beside him sat the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney), who also had to be consulted, and a little further along the row sat the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I sometimes wonder whether he did the whole thing on his own, and that is the reason they did not know, but certainly they did not know.
Well, what happened next? On January 12 again the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question and the minister brushed him off with a frivolity when he said he should have been satisfied with his own answer. Then the hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) asked a question, but he did not get very much information either. Then we come to January 17 and the minister proceeded to give an explanation, which appears on page 183 of Hansard. And, Mr. Speaker, imagine what misled him. It was the word "recent". The question was whether there had been any shipments recently. "Recent" is a hard word, subject to a number of definitions. That is what misled the minister. He said, of course, that it was not recently, it was back in June or July that those orders were given. Then, January 18, the Prime Minister was asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North whether he would cancel the export permits, and the Prime Minister said that no consideration had been given to that. Well, that was another step, and still we did not find out anything about those Harvards, except in a general way.
Then came Friday, January 20, and a lengthy explanation was given. It is an interesting one because one of the ministers who did not know anything about this, namely, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), said in part, as reported at page 344 of Hansard:
We are quite proud of our record and we are prepared to defend it at any time.
External Affairs
After the Prime Minister had given his explanation I asked him a very simple question, which appears at the bottom of page 345 of Hansard as follows:
Reverting to earlier discussion between the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister, would the Prime Minister tell the house whether the issue of export permits covering aircraft, explosives or other war material is decided at the cabinet level or on the basis of certain principles and, if so, what are those principles and when were they first communicated to the Department of Trade and Commerce?
The Prime Minister said:
Matters concerning the acceptance or otherwise of orders for any of that type of material are discussed at the cabinet level. But to my knowledge no orders are accepted before information has been communicated to those with whom it is sought to place the orders . . .
Then I asked this question:
When was the decision made regarding the export permit for aircraft for Egypt? At approximately what date did the cabinet determine that question?
And in reply to the inquiry when did the cabinet determine that question, the Prime Minister said:
It was some time in June of last year.
I then asked this question, which is unanswered today, as it was on January 20:
How is it that when the question was asked at the beginning of the session none of the ministers seemed to know anything about it? How is it they knew nothing about it?
At this point Mr. Fleming interjected:
I guess they were not at the cabinet meeting.
Then we come to the next step. Just picture this record of fumbling and bungling, if not evasion. The next step was that an order in council was passed. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said. This statement was made after 13 days of searching. And when the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced that an order in council had been passed, the other ministers sat and remained silent. When we asked for production of the order in council the Minister of Trade and Commerce informed us that he had made a mistake. He said, we do not pass orders in council on things like that.
What is this? Is this the manner in which we are to be treated in respect of information for which we ask on matters less serious than this? Today, however, the Prime Minister brings forward the final and revised version as of this date, and the possibility exists that in the days ahead there will be additional versions. The Prime Minister said it was by a ministerial order by the minister who thought he had an order in council passed. How often, Mr. Speaker, we have said that the cabinet enjoys the kind of

External Affairs
solidarity that it has exhibited today. What did they do? Who knows? If ever the loose practices of this cabinet have been revealed it has been in connection with this matter- everybody on board and nobody knowing where he is going; everyone with a different explanation. That is the parliamentary end of this matter. I say to the government in relation to external affairs and other matters that we in the opposition have our responsibilities to discharge. We expect-and have a right to expect-to be treated with candour. We were not treated with candour or frankness in this regard. There has been throughout this whole sorry spectacle an illustration of cabinet irresponsibility which cannot do anything else but shake the faith of those who like to believe that the information they receive, although it may not be all the information, does cover the actual facts.
The minister said on January 27 that, when aircraft were going to sensitive areas, ministerial concurrence was required of the ministers of external affairs, defence, and trade and commerce. The country in question was a sensitive area. The minister of external affairs so described it in the article published in Look magazine when he said:
In the Middle East, war could flare up any day between Israel and the Arab states. The Soviets are fanning the embers with arms shipments to Egypt (and incidentally with other communist governments, capturing about half of Egypt's foreign trade).
This statement indicates that the minister of external affairs regarded as dangerous the action of the U.S.S.R. in delivering munitions to the Middle East. He said that such shipments were "fanning the embers". I now ask the Prime Minister the question: Are you not doing the same thing when under such circumstances as have existed in the past six months you are employing this under-the-table method of delivering Har-vards and thus doing your part to fan those embers? I do not think it will always be that way. If conditions worsen there we can change our policy, but as long as the situation remains as it is today I say there can be no justification for condemning the U.S.S.R. for doing on a larger scale what we ourselves are doing.
As a result of the outstanding contribution made by its representatives in external affairs in every part of the world Canada has established a reputation as an objective nation whose interests are above the monetary considerations which actuate some nations. But as a result of the course taken by the government Canada's position of objectivity and moderation has been jeopardized. Having granted permits to export arms, the government has removed the most potent weapon

in Canada's arsenal of democracy, the moral weapon. Canada is no longer in the position where it can be a conciliator. It is no longer in the position where it can look on the other nations and say, "We are disinterested". Surely those things were thought of beforehand. Can the minister continue to rise in his seat and express Canada's moral indignation concerning the conduct of the U.S.S.R. in doing on a larger scale what Canada is doing? Surely the minister in his speech the other day did not intend to take virtually the same position as the U.S.S.R. when he said that, if we do not ship munitions to this country, the Russians will.
The things which have happened in the last few days indicate that the government knows that it has done wrong; surely it knows that. It is a piece of cynicism to say, "If we did not do so, the U.S.S.R. would have done it".
