Mr. Speaker, I suggest that by this conduct Canada's potentialities as conciliator and mediator have received a setback, as has Canada's reputation for selflessness, in the international world of today. I do not say that this condition should continue if world conditions change for the worse; then this matter can be reappraised. Having regard to the events of the past few weeks and what has been revealed here, I say-and I dislike to say it -that I think the conduct of this government deserves the condemnation of Canada for having, at a time like this, added its share of fuel to the embers which today are burning in the Middle East. I believe that this whole matter should be fully considered -and I know there have been alternative suggestions-by a parliamentary committee. Let us look into this. Let us find out the reasons for all the things that have taken

place, these bumbling, mumbling explanations, these detours and deviations.
It is unbelievable that out of something that is above board, as the government says, it should have been necessary for the government to build alibi after alibi. As one alibi was punctured, another found its place. Let me say this, too. This is something that is beyond partisanship; it is a matter affecting all Canadians; and we have always adopted that attitude. I should like to see some of the Liberal members speaking on this subject. I noticed that when the minister was in Moscow he made a very interesting statement there. He said, "When I return to Canada, I will discuss with other Canadian government members the question of forming a puppet theatre there". I do not know whether that is what this government has been trying to do since he got back but, if he could sit over there, he would not have to go to Moscow to see a puppet show.
I should like to mention one other thing. I believe with all my heart that the state of Israel must be preserved. As one walks through that state, one sees the foundations of civilization and one sees the landmarks of the conquerors, Persian, Assyrian, Roman, Crusader and Turk. One sees places holy to the three monotheistic religions. One sees a state in which a profound social revolution is taking place, vital and living, based on the imagination and inspiration of a dedicated people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to ask him a question? He has said that the state of Israel must, of course, be preserved at all costs. With that, everyone is in agreement. Will he agree, and does he say now, that arms should be sent to Israel to guarantee that preservation?
I shall return to that in a moment.
Oh.

I have never run away from any questions in the way the government runs away from questions from this side. Perhaps I may finish this, because I know my hon. friend, with his capacity for language, would expect me to complete the sentence. From the humblest to the greatest, this country, Israel, is engaged in the great adventure of creating a new democracy and achieving economic independence.
What should be done? What is this government doing about bringing into effect an international force to protect and assure the boundaries? What has it done? The other day there was a suggestion for the maintenance in their integrity of the boundaries under
External Affairs
an international arrangement very much in the same fashion as was dreamed of by Castlereagh over 130 years ago. What have they done about it? If conditions got worse and war broke out, then conditions as to the shipment of munitions would change, and all of us would change the views we have now; but until that time, on the basis of the words of the minister, remember that the sending of munitions is adding fire to the embers.
I suggest to my hon. friend who interrupted that one of the things he can do, with his influence in the United Nations, is to see to it that something in the nature of an international force is established to the end that this dangerous situation shall be obliterated. If it is not, and war breaks out there, we shall have war all over the world, for in every generation that area has seen the march of conquerors. It is almost like a beaten road for war.
What should we do? I say that we must face this problem courageously and manfully and not in the manner that we have seen here-a government hiding behind one explanation and then another, then throwing both overboard and finding refuge in still another. If the cabinet operates in other major matters in the same way that the Prime Minister revealed today and in the past few days, then indeed the question might well be asked, who leads, and whither?
My hon. friend mentioned NATO. The cement that has held NATO together has been fear. As I see it, the great danger today is this: that the removal of fear from the hearts of men will at the same time also remove that determination among nations to stand together. That is why I believe that article 2 deserves more intensive consideration now than ever in the past, in view of the new policy of the Soviet union. My hon. friend says we need today something of the spirit of faith, as I understood him, and I believe that. But what we need today is courage as well as faith, rather than challenging or truculent exhibitions of bravado such as "dancing to the brink of disaster." That type of expression is not conducive to peace. The minister has told us of his trip through the U.S.S.R. and to Moscow. The U.S.S.R. is using a new system. It is a kind of circus parade. Khrushchev and Bulganin go through India and they catch the imagination of the people. If only President Eisenhower had the health he had prior to last August! Would it not have been a great thing for him to go there and carry to those people something of his sincerity and the faith that he has in democracy, enjoying as he does the respect and admiration of peoples all over the world?

External Affairs
NATO may weaken. France has withdrawn three divisions to North Africa. German rearmament is slow. I have the figures here and rearmament is slower than was anticipated. Free nations cannot, as Eden said, negotiate from weakness. What is the new NATO policy? Three ministers went over there, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney). What policy was determined there? It was determined that a warning line was going to be built throughout Europe to which all of us would contribute. Has not the time come to reconsider the whole NATO set-up to the end that, since we are in a position in northern Canada of being in a potential front line, the general contribution of NATO should also be used within this country so that expenditures in northern Canada for defence will be part and parcel of the NATO defence for all the world?
Other matters will be dealt with by those who follow. We face, as the minister says, a new Soviet with a flexible, resourceful, ruthless policy. In the military field atomic energy seems to have resulted in a draw, but there remains one field that we have never yet explored to the extent that we should, the field of the hearts of men. We need a message to be given to the peoples in other parts of the world of what freedom means and the power that comes to men as they draw strength from the wells of freedom. We need the ability to explain that power. We need to mobilize their hearts by showing that our system is better than theirs.
The momentous task of the free world is not to falter in continuing to make the maximum effort for peace by negotiation, by the kind of thing the minister did when he talked face to face with Bulganin and Khrushchev. Negotiation might well have prevented the first world war. Sir Edward Grey said in his memoirs that if only the nations had continued to negotiate, the first world war would not have taken place. We must continue that negotiation. We must continue to provide mutual opportunities to meet those who are parliamentarians in other countries, particularly in the U.S.S.R. We must negotiate, but always with prudence and caution, and above all we must be on guard against unwarranted optimism, against becoming the manipulated victims of falsely created hopes on the part of the U.S.S.R. as that country wages its international war for the hearts of men.

I therefore move, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew):
That all the words after "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"in view of the present critical situation in the Middle East, this house expresses its strong disapproval of the government's policy of authorizing the shipment of munitions of war to countries in that area not within the NATO alliance: and also condemns the government for the lack of candour with which the matter has been dealt with in this house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Earlier in his remarks the hon. member for Prince Albert dealt with a declaration approved by the Supreme Soviet, dated February 9, 1955, in which are included three paragraphs at the end referring to what is presumably an invitation to exchange parliamentarians between the parliaments of the world. Certainly the hon. member was not aware that as recently as last Friday a meeting was held in my office of the whips of the four parties at which it was decided to study the matter. I think I should say in fairness to the whips that at that meeting an undertaking was given to the effect that the whips would report the subject matter to their various caucuses which, I understand, are to be held tomorrow morning. Another meeting is then to be held to deal further with the matter.

Mr. Speaker, the debate this afternoon is, of course, to some degree supplementary to the address which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made in the house last Tuesday, and a little later on in my speech I intend to take the opportunity to comment on the minister's remarks regarding the situation in the Middle East and to say something about the policy that I think Canada should support and forward both with the great powers and with the United Nations. But before I do that, Mr. Speaker,
I should like to say that I am very happy this afternoon to be able to compliment the Canadian delegation at the United Nations last autumn. I think that delegation, under the leadership of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), placed Canada in an excellent position and in a good light before the other nations of the world.
I am very happy indeed that the membership of the United Nations was expanded because I believe that sooner or later, if the United Nations is to become the kind of organization that we originally hoped it would be, it must become universal in character. Any step taken in that direction is, in my opinion, a right and proper move.
This afternoon we have heard a great deal about the disturbed situation of the world, about the determination of the Soviet union to expand its influence across the world in

various ways. I believe the minister is quite right when he tells the house that owing to the terror of the new weapons of war, particularly the hydrogen bomb, we are not likely to see the Soviet union embark on a shooting war-and of course we are not likely to see any nation outside of the Soviet union do so-which, with the modern weapons of war, would bring the world into ruins around us all. But I am inclined to think that the minister this afternoon rather underrated the potential influence of the Soviet union and the nations associated with the Soviet union in the competition which is developing in the field of economic aid. I think that what we are witnessing today is perhaps a diminution of the dangers of a military contest and that that military contest has been replaced by a new contest, namely a contest to win the world by means of economic and technical aid.
It may be said

as was said by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) -that the Soviet union has been unable to feed its people properly because of the failure of its agricultural plan. But the Russian people for centuries back, I was going to say-and I think that is probably the right thing to say-have been accustomed to an extremely low standard of living. From all the reports that we get, from what we heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) here and elsewhere and from what we heard from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) when he returned to Canada, undoubtedly those extremely low standards of living have been improved. The Russian people, seeing some slight improvement in the standards of living, are willing to forgo the great improvements that people in our countries would expect by great industrial expansion, so the Soviet union may be able to do more than make promises in the field of economic aid to the underprivileged nations of the world.
That brings me to the point that I really wish to make this afternoon, namely that the western nations-and among them Canada- must do very much more than we have been doing in assisting the under-privileged nations of the world to improve their standards of life and to go forward and therefore to resist those who would foment revolution and the institution of dictatorships. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I used the plural "dictatorships". I did so because it is not so long ago that a great country, in its distress, turned to a dictatorship of a different sort from that of the dictatorship of the communist party. I refer, of course, to the dictatorships that arose in the early 1930's in Europe, particularly that in Germany. To my
External Affairs
mind there is always a real danger of the emergence not only of communist dictatorships but of fascist dictatorships. I think they flourish on the same kind of fertile ground, namely the ground of misery and of want. When we look over the problem faced by the United Nations organizations in this field of economic aid, we find that it is a stupendous one. When we look at the resources that have been granted to the organizations that have been set up, we find that those resources are pitifully small.
Some time ago I jotted down some statements made by the United Nations secretary general of the technical aid organization. He is a gentleman whom many of us know well in Canada. I refer, of course, to Dr. Keenley-side. In Weekend magazine published by several newspapers in this country as a supplement on Saturdays, in the issue of July 9, 1955, he had some striking things to say. He said:
Grim figures illustrate the conditions under which a great part of the earth's population lives:
Over half the world's people are illiterate.
Most of the earth's inhabitants suffer from hunger most of the time.
Almost two-thirds of the people of the world have an average income of less than $100 a year compared with more than $1,500 in the United States.
The amount is only slightly less in Canada. In fact if we take the inflated figures of last year of the gross national product and divide it by our population last year, I think it will be found that we exceed that $1,500 figure. I know that when I was at the United Nations organization meeting in 1945 one of the statements that startled me-

-when I was on the committee that set up the economic and social council at San Francisco, was the statement that two-thirds of the people of the world-two out of every three persons-went to bed hungry every night. It was not necessarily the same two out of three but always two out of three. Generally speaking, that condition is no better today than it was in 1945.
That was in 1946; the fall of 1946.

Yes; in 1946 as well. Dr. Keenleyside went on to say this:
More than half are ill (500 million suffer from malaria; almost the entire land mass between the tropics is afflicted with yaws-
That is a dreadful tropical disease which a small amount of penicillin will suffice to cure.
-400 million have venereal diseases; between 3 million and 5 million a year die from tuberculosis-[DOT] and that is just the beginning of the list.

External Affairs
Much has been said about what is being done already through various schemes of assistance to under-developed areas. There is the United Nations technical assistance program, the Colombo plan, the Point Four program in the United States and the like. But the discussion of these organizations at the United Nations and the numbers of words used far exceed the amount of money appropriated to do the kind of jobs that these organizations are endeavouring to do.
Then he went on to say this:
We could go on for 200 years at the present rate without producing the effects that are wanted.
Then he remarks on the United Nations technical assistance program. He said:
It originally envisaged the spending of $25 million to $35 million in the first 18-month period during 1950-51, and an expansion to above $50 million to $100 million annually within a few years.
How near are we to that target? Because of the reluctance of some governments-and may I add because of the reluctance of governments like Canada's government-to give a greater lead in appropriations for this cause our contribution is to some extent minimized. We are all inclined to say that on a per capita basis we should contribute this much if somebody else contributes that much. I am glad that a year ago we increased our contribution from $1 million to $1,500,000 a year. But how petty that amount really is, as I shall show in a moment, I hope, in comparison with other expenditures that we make.
The article goes on to say:
Because of the reluctance of some governments to contribute on a sufficient scale, the sum of $25 million was achieved for the first time in 1954. But the amount of money available has not increased at all in proportion to the requests from the various governments for assistance.
Some western nations are spending $100 on military defence for every $1 spent on aid to the underdeveloped areas. While military preparation is a first requirement under today's conditions, this proportion of spending strikes many observers as being badly out of balance.
What is our own record in that same field? Let us look at our expenditures, and I take them from the public accounts for 1954-55 tabled in this house. Our total economic aid of every sort, according to the public accounts, was $29,016,824.86. What did we spend for national defence? We spent $1,665,968,960.31. This amount does not include the defence production expenditures which were made in addition to the figure I have just placed on the record. What would economic aid be as a percentage of the military defence figure which I have just noted? It is 1-74 per cent. Our population on July 31, 1955, was estimated by the dominion bureau of statistics to be 15,637,000. Our

economic aid amounted to $1.86. per capita. On the other hand, for military expenditures, not counting defence production, we spent $106.54 per capita.
Now I contend, Mr. Speaker, that we are not going to be successful in winning the world for the kind of democracy and freedom in which we believe and which we enjoy in our western countries. We may urge different steps in democratic development, and all the rest of it: we may visualize different stages in our evolution from one form of economic structure to another; but in our western countries we all value personal freedom and human liberty. We want to see that extended across the world. My belief is that we are not going to win this struggle unless we are prepared to do far more than we have been doing by way of economic aid. I am very glad to note that the Colombo plan aid is to be increased this year. However, it is not particularly substantial when compared with our wealth and compared with our expenditures in other fields. But it is a step in the right direction, and I am very glad indeed to see it undertaken.
I noted the articles that were written by that brilliant young journalist who travels and reports from time to time for the Ottawa Journal, Mr. I. Norman Smith. I read his articles when he was sending them from the Soviet union and the Far East. I read the speech which he delivered before the Canadian Club in this city some two or three weeks ago. In that address he had this to say:
Yet the Colombo plan is virtually all Canada is doing about Asia, the area Mr. Pearson says may be history's most important crucible at this time.
1 do not relish saying what I am about to say, but I must say it. I have found that many Canadians seem almost to resent the poverty of Asian people. It embarrasses us, we look the other way if they beg and say to ourselves that we cannot stand beggars. But if they do not beg, and instead seem to keep company with arrant nationalists or even communists, then we call them fellow travellers and shut up our doors.
Well, that is one man's opinion and it may not be entirely correct. But undoubtedly we are complacent. There is no room for complacency in the kind of world in which we live today, a world in which millions of people are hungry, sick and illiterate; millions of people who may very easily be enticed into the communist orbit. I am thinking particularly of India, because I feel India is the key country in Asia from our point of view. If India should fall behind China in improving the standards of living, if the Chinese under their dictatorship, no matter how harsh it may be, are able over the next 10, 15 or 25 years, to outpace India in improving the

standards of life in that part of Asia, then the communist orbit will be extended over a vast majority of the human race.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, we have every facility for assisting in improving conditions in these countries. The other afternoon I mentioned the necessity of our building up our educational system so that we might not be outpaced in the field of science. May I just say in passing that when I speak of science and technical education I do not believe, of course, that we should endeavour only to make men scientists or technicians. I think the basis of even a scientific and technical education is a good, what we call a liberal, education. I think the humanities are as essential to the scientists or technicians as they are to any other calling or profession. We have to develop technicians and scientists, not only for ourselves, but we have to be able to provide them in greater numbers to the backward countries of the world.
I am not saying how much we should appropriate. I am not saying we can appropriate a billion dollars out of the defence budget or something of that sort. But I am saying we can do many times what we are doing now in order to preserve ourselves, our safety and the future welfare of the land in which we live. I am very happy indeed to see that we are making a slight improvement in our contribution to the Colombo plan. A year and a half ago I would have liked to have seen Canada support the proposal for the special United Nations fund. A proposition was put forward that, in addition to all the other agencies, we should set up a new organization with a capitalization, if my memory serves me correctly, of about $250 million-not Canada alone but the nations together-to assist in the development of the underdeveloped countries. This was not necessarily an organization which would have within it only publicly appropriated funds by parliaments. Private capital was to be invited to assist in the establishment of the fund and the working out of its details. I was with the delegation at New York when that came up, and I was sorry to know that our government could not see its way clear at that time to support the proposal. I know it will come before the United Nations from time to time and I hope that sooner or later the government may see its way clear not only to take part but perhaps to give some leadership in that field.
We have heard a great deal about these matters from time to time and I wanted to emphasize them again this afternoon because as I have said-and I want to repeat it-the struggle that is going on in the world is not going to be won on the battlefields of the
External Affairs
world; it is going to be won to the extent that we can win over to the democratic ideals that we hold in common with those associated with us and to our side those countless people of Asia and of Africa who today need our help and our aid.
I now want to say something about the situation in the Middle East. I thought the minister made a very excellent windup to his speech last Tuesday. I thought he was rather unnecessarily harsh in his criticism of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) because the hon. gentleman had brought something before the house that he considered to be of importance at that time. We all realize that what he did was done in good faith. Because of the situation with which the world is faced in the Middle East that area has become the danger spot of the world. We had Korea; we had Formosa. Now we have the Middle East. I agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that it would be indeed a great world tragedy, a great loss to the world, if the newly emerging democratic state of Israel were to be destroyed. It is the only state in that area of the world with institutions like our own; it is the only state in that part of the world with leadership of a democratic sort; it is the only state in that part of the world with an institution like the institution in which we are assembled today. A parliamentary institution modelled very largely along our lines; and indeed, as I know from talking to the clerk of the Knesset, with procedures that are very similar to the procedures that we use in this parliament.
We look back over the years and we find that the Israel-Arab armistice of 1949 has been followed ever since by hostility from the surrounding countries. They resent the establishment of the new state of Israel in that area. So great was the danger that in 1950 the three powers issued the tripartite agreement or declaration, Britain, the United States and France. They attempted at that time to check the drift to actual war. Their declaration, of course, was designed at that time to stabilize conditions there. How? Well, first of all, of course, by a warning that if Israel were attacked there would be immediate intervention; that no party, neither Israel nor the Arab states, should try to alter the boundaries as they had then been drawn. In addition, they tried to maintain a balance there by restricting the inflow of arms into the whole area. But since 1950 various events have happened. First of all, we had the evacuation of the Suez canal area by the United Kingdom, which gave to the Arab nations, and primarily to Egypt, access to

External Affairs
many modern weapons and arms. Since then, of course, other weapons of war have been shipped to Egypt; but the most alarming thing that has happened to upset the balance in that area is the recent agreement between the Egyptians and the Czechs under which, with the assistance of the Soviet union, vast supplies of modern arms are going into Egypt, and the threat becomes ever greater, not only of an outbreak of war in that area, but if war should come and no assistance be forthcoming, the state of Israel might conceivably be eliminated.
Those of us who have been to Israel are well aware of the fact that in some places the distance between Israel's boundary and the sea is less than twelve miles. If my memory serves me rightly, in one place it is around six miles. How easy it would be for an enemy to cut across, divide the country and destroy it. They have, as those of us who have been there have seen, a very intelligent and well-trained armed force.
I am not suggesting that we should foment an arms race in that area. Indeed, I find it very difficult to think how an arms race could be fomented in that area under the conditions that exist there, where arms are being poured into Egypt from Czechoslovakia and from communist countries and similar arms denied to Israel. We could not conceivably pour in arms at the same rate, nor could Israel arrange to purchase them. And yet, of course, when you look back over the last twenty or thirty years, you wonder how a nation can exist unless it has firm guarantees from the great powers that are interested in its survival. I hope that when Sir Anthony Eden is here next week-and for certain this problem will be discussed; it may not be discussed publicly but it will be discussed privately-the minister will use his very best endeavour to get him and, as far as the minister can influence the United States, the state department of that country, to make a declaration saying that if war is started in that area by either side immediately the great powers will intervene on the side opposite to the aggressor nation to stop the conflict and to prevent war.
I should like 'to see the United States and Great Britain do that. France, of course is so involved in North Africa that I am not even suggesting it participate, I quite agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that what we need is a security force under the United Nations but we do not have it. We cannot rely on a force that does not exist to preserve peace. That, of course, is not logical nor sound and it certainly could not be effective if not in being.

I do not know whether or not the great powers would see to it that the state of Israel were not left defenceless. I would not send into Israel offensive equipment in the nature of bombers or something of that sort, but I doubt very much if the nations of the world can afford to see Israel threatened and inadequately armed, bearing in mind the relative proportions of population in Israel and the surrounding Arab states. There is one person in Israel for every 30 Arabs in the Arab states and the latter are well armed and well equipped now. I do not think the second suggestion I implied would be necessary if the great powers said, "We are going to see to it that no war starts in that area and we are going to stop aggression immediately, no matter from which side it comes".
I cannot conceive of Israel being imbued with a warlike spirit to try to drive back the 30 million Arab people from its borders. If Israel should attempt it they should be stopped from doing it. If, on the other hand, Egypt and the Arab states move against Israel, then I think that the great powers might make it abundantly clear that they would intervene immediately and stop the conflict. I think all of us in this house agree that it is essential that the state of Israel shall continue to exist and prosper.
I am going to move an amendment to the amendment because I think the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Prince Albert does not take into consideration conditions that might arise from time to time. I feel his amendment is too binding on this nation and that we should have some latitude, that our hands should not be tied too tightly in connection with the situation that exists there.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein immediately after the word "alliance" the following words:
"without at the same time making sure that peace in that area would be guaranteed either by the United Nations or by the powers that signed the tripartite agreement of 1950, namely the United States, the United Kingdom and France."
It seems to me in that way we safeguard ourselves against possible misunderstanding. We do not say that under all circumstances we would be averse to supplying means of defence to a nation which we assisted in establishing. One of the things which pleased me when I was in Jerusalem and various other parts of Israel was to discover the high regard in which Canada is held by that country because of the work our minister of external affairs did on the commission some years ago, because

of the work done by Mr. Justice Rand, whose name stands high in the regard of the people of that country, and because of the work that is being done today-or was being done when I was there-by General Burns. Those three names, if not universally known, are known among the people who lead that nation and among others who take an interest in affairs. They hold Canada in high esteem. We should leave ourselves room in which to move so that if the existence of a country which we helped to establish were threatened we would not be so bound that our government could not take effective steps to give immediate aid in the situation.
My time has just about run out, Mr. Speaker. I should like to have said something about the European situation and NATO. I am glad to know that those who went overseas last year to meet with other parliamentary delegations to discuss and examine NATO came back feeling pleased that they were afforded the opportunity of visiting there and brought back much useful information. I believe these inter-parliamentary meetings, whether they are commonwealth meetings, united nations meetings or other parliamentary gatherings, serve a useful purpose. I am glad to know that the parliamentarians from Canada who visited NATO last year feel that the expedition was worth while and that they were able to advance the interests of our country and of the NATO cause by their attendance at the meeting.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome the opportunity, presented at this early date in the session, of discussing some of the very important aspects of the present international situation.
With reference to the international scene, the speech from the throne intimated that some developments have been welcome as releasing tensions in certain parts of the world while other unfortunately have had the contrary effect. Also in the speech this afternoon of the Secretary of State for External Affairs we had presented to us in a very clear manner the conditions that exist in various parts of our world. This helped to clarify some matters and to answer some questions that have been of concern to us.
We, of course, are in the position where we are not able to look at these things at first
External Affairs
hand but we must glean our information concerning world affairs from various sources, and we are quite ready to admit some of them may not be reliable in every respect. However, after considerable study of the various situations and after comparing reports and making inquiries in various fields, there are a number of conclusions at which we are justified in arriving.
After we analyse the whole picture, it would appear that the prospects for stability and peace in the world are no brighter than they were some months ago. The cold war, apparently, is still on. Tensions in various sectors continue to hamper the efforts of men of good will in their quest for grounds for mutual confidence and understanding. The leaders of the nation have so far failed to find that common ground which, I believe, is essential to international peace and harmony.
I am not saying that the situation is hopeless. I would not want to think that that were so. We are not saying that it is hopeless and that therefore further efforts are more or less in vain. But the very fact that dangers still obtain, the very fact that tensions still exist, the very fact that efforts up to the present time have not yielded the results we had hoped for, those very facts must urge us on to even greater efforts towards peace and security. There must be a greater concentration and dedication of our resources, intellectual, moral, spiritual, economic, and in every other sense, to the task of establishing and maintaining a society in which justice, equity, peace, mutual understanding and freedom may be preserved for all the peoples of the world.
It would be impossible to deal with all the many matters of urgent concern. A number of them have already been dealt with in the debate today. It would seem that the numbers of important matters are increasing rather than diminishing. As has been pointed out, in some areas of our world these problems are of such a nature that they could, it seems, at any moment result in limited, if not widespread, conflict.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs dealt at length with the continued threat and the fact of communist aggression and expansion. I do not think it is necessary to review the stages by which a large portion of the world's population has been brought under the tyranny of this despotic and diabolical system. Suffice it at the moment to say that its spread has been rapid and far too extensive. We find our world divided into two camps: the east and the west. It has been referred to as a conflict for the minds and for the very souls of men. Certainly, when we

External Affairs
look at it from that viewpoint, we can understand the magnitude, and the importance, of the task that confronts the statesmen of the world.
Last summer the world looked forward with a great deal of expectation to the conference that was called to meet in Geneva. The leaders of the four nations met there together to try to solve, or to get a deeper understanding of, the problems that confronted these four nations. It was suggested that the purpose of that meeting was to explore the extent of the change in the Soviet policy and also to deal with a number of other matters of great concern.
The Toronto Star in an article outlined the proposed eight topics for that discussion as set forth by President Eisenhower. German reunification was the first one. The second was an east-west security system in which a united Germany would have the right to choose its own allies. The third was the right of the Soviet satellites to choose their own form of government. The fourth was the tearing down of "communication and human" barriers between the Soviet union and the west. The fifth was an end to subversion by international communism. The sixth was limitation of armaments. The seventh was a higher standard of living for underdeveloped nations. The eighth was the development for peaceful uses of atomic energy.
When we look at those items which had been placed on the proposed agenda, we realize some of the problems that were confronting those four leaders as they met on that occasion. Those various matters that were broached were, of course, of a very controversial nature, as we can all readily understand. As I say, the world had looked forward with some expectation to that meeting, hoping that some good would be brought out of seeming chaos. But, sad to say, that was not the case.
Much was said about a change in the attitude of the Soviet leaders, about their smiles and their friendly attitude. Some of the newspapers of our country went out of their way to stress the happy and congenial spirit with which the Soviet leaders had approached that gathering, cavorting like tourists, appearing almost unaccompanied when compared with some of the western leaders who had their bodyguards, and so on. Yet we find that the result was negligible. Some have said that great things were accomplished; some have said that some good things were accomplished; but in the over-all picture it would not seem that the results had been too worth while.
TMr. Patterson.]
The Soviet leaders are ever declaring their determination to work for peace. They constantly proclaim themselves as the champions of peace, the champions of freedom and of liberty. But certainly, as has been stated today, their actions do not prove that that is necessarily so. We think of the recent trip that premier Bulganin and party boss Khrushchev made to India and Burma. They seemed to go out of their way to make statements which tended to stir up animosity. It seemed as though they deliberately set themselves to make charges that would cause the western powers to react in a very unfavourable way. I am going to refer to several of them a little later, but I would suggest that the words of Mr. Khrushchev especially were far from words of peace. Their actions on these occasions were not the actions of men who were sincerely and honestly striving to ease world tensions. They certainly were not designed or calculated in any way to foster friendship and good will on the part of the western democracies at least.
There are hopes expressed at times that the communist tactics or their over-all plan and objective may change, but I think their plan and objective still remain the same. Communism plans world domination. Their program has been announced, progress is being made, and their plans seem almost so fantastic that it is hard to believe they are really setting out on that course. But I think the very fact we find it difficult to believe that the program is as outlined adds to the danger in which we find ourselves. And so we think of the progress of communism. We think of the nations that have been brought under the control of the Russian regime, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, the Ukraine, Poland, Czechoslovakia, yes, China and others. We think of their endeavours in Korea and Indo-China and it would seem that the fact is proven that communism has set its course and that its objective is still the domination of all the peoples of the world.
It has been stated that communism in its attempts to enslave the world takes one step backward and two steps forward. I am inclined to believe that, although we are opposed to communist aggression and expansion, we take one step forward and two steps backwards. I like to look back through the records of the recent past and find what some have said with reference to our attitude or what our attitude should be towards communism. In the Vancouver Province of November 30, 1955, there is a Canadian Press report from the United Nations, New York, reading as follows:
Canada's external affairs minister Pearson has warned that the so-called "soft" Russian approach to world affairs may prove more dangerous to the west than Stalin hostility. In an address to the

U.N. correspondent association, Pearson cautioned against any tendency to relax western defences and urged the people to gird for a long grind of "'competitive coexistence." . .	. He said "competitive coexistence" may prove more hazardous for the west than the cold war tactics of Stalin's regime. "We must make sure that relaxation of tension does not mean relaxation of effort."
I may say I was pleased to note in the speech the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made today that he still holds that same view. There were times when I almost thought he was going to back track, but I felt a little reassured today to know that he is still facing in the same direction and taking the same attitude with respect to this very serious situation. I should like to refer to an article by George Meany, president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., found in the issue of the Ensign of January 14. The article reads:
Too many in the free world fail to see the real nature of communism as the mortal foe of everything that we hold dear, of every moral and spiritual value. Too many in the free world are still prisoners of the illusion that communism is, historically speaking, a progressive system- extreme liberalism temporarily making bad mistakes. Actually communism represents darkest reaction. It is an anti-social system in which there are imbedded some of the worst features of savagery, slavery, feudalism and life-sapping exploitation manifested in the industrial revolution of early day capitalism.
He goes on to make some other very striking statements with regard to communism and what our attitude should be in response to its challenge. I should like to refer again to an article entitled, "This is Our Foreign Policy" by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in Weekend magazine of January 28, 1956, and I like to think that this is the policy of the present government. Speaking of the Soviet rulers and their assaults on NATO and so on, he has this to say:
Their hope is our challenge, and it is going to be a hard one to meet and defeat. Adequate military defence alone will not do it, though it is essential. Close political co-operation between the free nations; flexible and imaginative diplomacy; economic health; social progress; sympathy for and assistance to the underdeveloped free countries, especially in Asia; all these are a part of the answer to this aggressive challenge of international communism. As such they reinforce Canada's security.
