There has been some discussion relative to the Middle East situation. In his statement this afternoon the minister did not touch on that matter because he had already made a statement in this regard just a short time ago. I would consider that this is the most sensitive of all the areas at the present time. It is an area in which reside two peoples between whom a feud has been carried on for generations. It was my privilege to be at the United Nations general assembly in 1954. There I heard the representatives of some of the Arab countries and also the delegate from Israel speak in the plenary sessions. Charges and countercharges were made. Yet it was not difficult to sense the feeling of animosity and, on the part of some, of hatred toward the other side on this particular question at that particular time. I would therefore just make my remarks in this respect very brief.
We recall that some time ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) stopped in and had a visit with the leader of Egypt. At that time it was regretted that it was not possible for him to stop in and visit the leaders of the state of Israel at the same time because at that time matters were in an extremely delicate position. However, he has already made the statement that in the near future a visit will be paid to Israel as well. We certainly appreciate that statement because, human nature being what it is and international moves being subject to political interpretations at all times, even these smallest matters must be given due consideration.
As to the Middle East problem, we have had called to our attention a number of things that constitute matters of friction. There is the refugee problem. We are not going into an explanation of the situation with regard to the refugees. I believe that every hon. member in the house is aware of the conditions. There we find a great many refugees herded together in camps and kept in idleness. That is a situation that constitutes a festering sore in that particular part of the world. I should like to suggest that the time

has come when some definite decision should be taken relative to this particular situation.
These people are being sustained by funds from the United Nations Organization. Canada is making her contribution to those funds and is assisting in the maintenance of those people in the camps. But in view of the fact that so much money is being spent and that apparently no endeavour is being made to rehabilitate these people, at least to any extent, it would seem to me that the time has come when a decision ought to be made that the moneys that are given from here on, or after a certain date, must be used for the rehabilitation of these people and not just to maintain them in these camps where they are deteriorating and where they are kept in idleness. There may be reasons why they are being kept there. But certainly I think I am expressing the feelings of this group, at any rate, when I say that our government ought to make some statement to the effect that money that is given from now on must be used for the rehabilitation of these people.
We understand that a considerable number have been accepted back and have been integrated into the economy of the state of Israel. I do not think it is too much to suggest that those who remain should now become the responsibility of the Arab countries, that they should be willing to extend the hand of help and welcome and be willing to integrate the remainder of these people into the economies of the respective Arab nations. I think that this would do a great deal to assist in the solution of the problem that we find in that area.
There is the problem of the boundary. There is the problem of the use of the various water resources of the country. All of these things have their particular point of emphasis. But I think there is something that is behind all of these things. There is the major problem. I should like to call attention to an article in the January 30, 1956, issue of Time magazine. There may be one or two of the words in this article that I do not pronounce correctly, but I shall give the English version of them. The article is in the foreign affairs section under the heading "The Middle East". It is entitled "Holy War".
"Egypt does not want a war." So says Egypt's Premier Abdel Nasser, leading statesman of the Arab world. But the supreme spiritual voice of all Islam in effect denies that protestation. From Cairo's 1,000-year-old A1 Azhar university, the committee of senior Ulema-
The footnote refers to the "Ulema" as:
A body of scholars trained in Islamic law and religion that has long been recognized as the highest Moslem authority in matters of faith.

Let me read that sentence again:
From Cairo's 1,000-year-old A1 Azhar university, the committee of senior Ulema solemly confirmed a jihad (holy war) against Israel.
The fatwa (ruling), a pronouncement having almost the same force for Moslems as a papal encylical for Roman Catholics, decrees that for a moslem to recognize the state of Israel would be to condone an act of robbery.
Then farther down it says:
. . . any peace with Israel that includes recognition of its existence as a state in Palestine "is against faith".
So you see, Mr. Speaker, it goes back beyond some of these problems that appear on the surface, and it is based upon the fact that the Arab world is not prepared, under any circumstances, to recognize the right of Israel to exist as a nation. There, we see the problem all the statesmen of the world are facing in their endeavour to stabilize the situation. I say it is a delicate situation. Any action that is taken by the United Nations or by individual nations, and especially by Canada, must be based upon sound principles, be absolutely fair and must not in any way tend to upset the present balance, if there is a balance. Nor must it tend to add to the tensions already so evident in that troubled area.
I wanted to make a few remarks about the technical assistance program and the Colombo plan. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) placed on the record this afternoon some of the figures relative to the need of the peoples of the world. Their economic conditions were outlined very clearly and they impressed upon us the fact that if we are going to discharge our moral obligations in this world then we must recognize the needs of our fellow men, regardless of where they may be found. We do appreciate the contributions that have been made and are being made by Canada through these various funds, but certainly we feel that they can be extended, they can be increased, for in that way we would assist tremendously in the solution of those problems that are so real to a great portion of our world.
I think we must help those people in the underdeveloped nations to help themselves. We must be willing to share with them the good things that we enjoy. We must increase our contribution and above all it seems to me that the assistance we give must be governed not by political or economic considerations only but by a sincere concern for the welfare of our fellow men.
I was very pleased that in the meeting at Geneva the President of the United States made a clear declaration regarding the satellite nations of Europe. He reminded the Soviet rulers that in order to fulfil their
External Affairs
obligations and fulfil their promises they would be required to grant to those people the freedom to choose their own form of government and to enjoy political freedom and liberty.
I did want to refer to several statements by Mr. Khrushchev while he was in India and Burma. I have a copy of the Soviet bulletin in which those speeches are recorded. When the minister is winding up this debate, I should like him to state whether or not the Canadian embassy in the U.S.S.R. is free to publish and circulate material to the same extent that the Soviet embassy does in this country. These bulletins are very enlightening. I just want to read one or two.
But, continued N. S. Khrushchev, we have condemned and we condemn the colonial system, and hold that the sooner it is done away with the better as it is a profoundly unjust, man-hating system. The sooner the peoples of colonial countries are freed from it, the better. We are the most sincere friends of those who fight against colonial enslavement and colonial dependence.
I should like Mr. Khrushchev to turn around and have a look at some of the countries that are now under communist domination. We think of the satellite countries. We think perhaps of the subjugated nations, those that now have lost their political identity and been swallowed up by communist imperialism. I should like Mr. Khrushchev to answer the question whether he believes in freedom for the European nations as well as for the Asian nations. Certainly, I think that thought should be brought to his attention. If they are going to talk about freedom and liberty for nations, then they are going to be expected to loosen the shackles, break down the iron curtain and give these people an opportunity to make their own choice. Only then can we understand and believe in the sincerity of their proclamation that they are in favour of freedom and liberty around the world.
Today we reaffirm our faith in the principle of self-determination of people. We say the true government of a people is that which they have voluntarily chosen and to which they have pledged allegiance. God grant that such liberty and freedom may be the possession of every nation and every people in the world.

There are manifestations in the life of each nation, Mr. Speaker, which generally indicate its aspirations and tendencies. As for our own country, the most recent efforts for world peace by our statesmen clearly evoke for Canada a renewed testimonial. Our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) circled the globe; two of our ministers' flew to Russia, and our

External Affairs
Minister of National Health and Welfare Mr. Martin) fathered the admission of 16 lew countries into the family of nations, all n the hope that the cause of peace in the vorld would be advanced.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the wholesomest nanifestations of a people's genuine desire o live in the spirit of those who, throughout he ages, proclaimed peace on earth and good vill toward mankind. A similar spirit prevailed and manifested itself at the first Geneva conference. The peace tempo was ncreasing, but shortly afterward we were funned by the realization that the Russians vere again merely appeasing our peace lunger while secretly continuing to press heir diabolic plans. They lulled us into lelieving that the Russian bear had dulled ts claws, and now brazenly attempt to do so iy their peace-manoeuvring in Washington ast week, while scheming, no doubt, some )ther nefarious plans.
This scheming, Mr. Speaker, is now directed iy the two enigmatic personalities of Khrushchev and Bulganin, as was so very fioquently stated by the hon. member for Eraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), who spoke a :ew moments ago. The one, Khrushchev is a ilind zealot and a ruthless communist. His ippearance, strangely enough, spells out to he eye the reflection of his personality. The ither is a benign-looking gentleman, but ;ogether, they are the mailed fist in the velvet 'love, and in biblical language, they combine he voice of Jacob with the hands of Esau.
This is confirmed, Mr. Speaker, by the 'act that during the wining and dining, the mailing and the hand-shaking at the Geneva inferences, plans were secretly being made :or the invasion of the Middle East and Africa ay communist ideology.
It is historic knowledge that since the nghteenth century Russia has been aspiring ;o secure a passage through the Bosphorus md the Dardanelles to the Mediterranean. They have now virtually pole-vaulted over \sia Minor and secured reasonable access to he Mediterranean, the Suez canal and the :ontinent of Africa.
The Russians plan cunningly years in advance. Shortly after the second world war, hr example, they laid claims to ports in Italian Libya and Eritrea. In this way they served notice on the world that they seek an opportunity of entering this virgin territory. Since this plan could best be achieved hrough the Middle East, she eagerly sought an ally in this area. The scheme became more obvious, Mr. Speaker, from the Soviet support given to Arab claims at the Bandung conference and the subsequent invitation to
[Mr. Crestohl.)
Colonel Nasser to visit Russia. If we add to this the recent stepped-up vigour of the Russian espousal, without qualification, of all Arab claims in the United Nations we have a clear-cut indication of her eagerness for an alliance with Egypt.
She then proceeds through the back-door use of Czechoslovakia, and provides arms to Egypt as well as personnel to train Egyptians in the use of aircraft, armaments and even submarines. These agents flock into Egypt, which is the front-door entrance to Africa, and from there they have easy access to the rest of that continent.
I have personally, Mr. Speaker, seen this infiltration at work in the heart of Africa while on a visit to Ethiopia last year. Communist literature was openly and brazenly displayed in Ethiopian ministerial offices. Embassies and compounds of legations close to Russian influence are amongst the largest in the country, and I wondered why. I heard more Russian spoken in Addis Ababa than any other European language. I was both astonished and fearful.
The menace, Mr. Speaker, is very great. Mr. John Gunther, noted author, has the following to say on the subject in his recently published book, "Inside Africa", and I quote briefly:
This fabulous continent is democracy's last frontier. It is the richest prize on earth and is defenceless in a period of cold war. Already there are areas where the communists are almost in a position to take over the nationalist movement. If communism is ever let loose on the intolerably poor and crushed in the submerged regions of the continent, a development might arise like that in China. And we will have lost Africa, as China and Asia have been lost.
To continue to be unrealistic in the face of this admonition, Mr. Speaker, is being ostrich-like in our need to recognize the studied determination and procedures of communism, not only to invade but to capture the whole of Africa. There is, for example, amongst many other manoeuvres the vigorous propaganda assault now actually in process seriously threatening the security of East Africa.
Cairo radio, in line with Egypt's new offensive, opened this assault dramatically about the middle of last October with these words spoken in Swahili, which is the language that reaches 20 million Africans, and I quote:
"The Mau Mau revolt, in which white arms defeated black courage, must be revived, not only in Kenya, but in the entire continent, and must go on until Africa belongs to the Africans."
Political observers, Mr. Speaker, familiar with communist tactics, openly declare that no subversive material aimed at Africa in the past has ever reached this blatant and

dangerous level. That, Mr. Speaker, is a very distressing fact, but unfortunately that is not all. Tanganyika and Uganda are also extremely jittery, and the white communities are exerting efforts to provide powerful antidotes over their radio stations at Dar-es-Salaam and Kampala.
If antidotes are necessary, it is a sign that the poison is already penetrating. But what is more disturbing, Mr. Speaker, than even that is that these deliberate and inflammatory appeals are also delivered in Arabic. It is no accidental coincidence that both the appeal in Swahali and in Arabic was launched immediately after Egypt concluded her arms deal with the Soviet.
It is abundantly clear that this is part of a bargain that Egypt entered into with the Soviet, and it becomes apparent that her campaign against the white man is the price she has to pay for the military aid she receives from Russia and her satellites.
It is my conviction, Mr. Speaker, that Egypt wants this military aid because Mr. Nasser, in his dream of becoming the Moslem Bismarck, has some aggressive ideas of his own, and Israel is being used only as a decoy for the purpose of securing armed power.
I foresee, for example, that apart from Egypt's desire to dominate the entire Arab world, as Nasser proclaimed the other day, one of the things she no doubt expects from her alliance with Russia is the immediate realization of her aim to acquire the Sudan, which is now in no position to resist Egypt's so-called protective invasion, especially in the face of her newly-acquired desert tanks and armaments. This would bring Russian influence to the borders of Ethiopia. With the pressure from both Egypt and Russia, Haile Selassie, in his desire to preserve his throne, would then be an easy victim for a deal. All this would place Russia strategically in a good position to advance her plan for a cold war invasion of Africa.
This program, Mr. Speaker, could never be realized by Russia without her finding a base on the African coast of the eastern Mediterranean, and this explains her anxiety for the alliance with Egypt. This also reveals to some degree the real dimensions of what appears to be an innocuous arms deal with Czechoslovakia. Newsweek of November 28, 1955, reports most disquieting information pointing a red arrow at the very heart of the Middle East itself all of which developed on the heels of this new alliance. And what do we find in the Middle East? Syria is on the verge of a red arms agreement. In Cairo, Egyptian and Soviet spokesmen declared that Saudi Arabia had already signed for the acquisition of communist arms and is now in the midst
External Affairs
of a Soviet-inspired bribery scandal causing disturbances in the country itself. Yemen, which is in a dispute with Great Britain over Aden, also seeks Soviet arms. Egypt offers Soviet arms to Jordan, one of Great Britain's hopes in the Middle East, and Jordan shows signs of succumbing to Egyptian pressures. There you see, Mr. Speaker, that the supply of arms to Egypt involves not just the supply of arms to Egypt but the supply of arms to every Arab country in the Middle East. I urge most cautious, profound and courageous consideration of all these facts. They are not trivial and show manifestations of being very foreboding and very dangerous.
I admit my inadequacies, Mr. Speaker, in not being as knowledgeable about these events as either Washington, London or Paris, but the pattern seems so clear that one does not have to be an expert to be frightened by these developments. In fact, the New York Times of October 15, 1955, very poignantly and frankly declared that when Mr. Dulles received the news that Russia was unloading Soviet bloc arms in the Middle East he himself had a conniption fit. The rest of the civilized world should certainly feel no better about it.
Our alarm is even more startling when we are told that near Alexandria on the Mediterranean, a vast area, consisting of tens of square miles, has been reserved for the gathering and conditioning of incalculable quantities of armaments including tanks, jet fighters, jet bombers and submarines. The section is cautiously guarded and looms as a jumping off point. In addition, Mr. Speaker, there are thousands of Russians in greatly increasing numbers swarming into Arab countries under various guises. The combination of these arms and agents in the Middle East is ominous and I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that this procedure is painfully reminiscent of Russian tactics in North Korea and China. First she armed them and then sent in thousands of so-called experts and technicians and when they were good and ready catapulted them into a war.
It is puerile to believe that the Russians are providing such vast quantities of arms to the Egyptians solely for their defence against an assault by the tiny state of Israel. Let us not be duped by the Egyptian cry of "wolf". Israel, with a population of one and a half million and an area of a mere 8,000 square miles, by comparison with 50 million Arabs and an area of 2,600,000 square miles, does not merit the dubious compliment of having to provide against them the vast armaments, aircraft and submarines presently being gathered in Egypt.

External Affairs
Much larger game is the objective. The western world must recognize this quickly and promptly challenge it not merely by talk nor by appeasement and certainly not by sacrificing important human values and principles which form the cornerstone of our civilization.
The Arab fear of invasion by the tiny state of Israel and its handful of people is universally recognized as being ludicrous. The reverse is more likely and more threatening.
Israel lives under a sword of Damocles in the form of the constant Arab threat of annihilation. On January 9, 1954, King Saud called upon the Arab world to wage a holy war against Israel, and to sacrifice 10 million Arabs if necessary, in order to destroy it completely.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) a few moments ago also referred to the students in Cairo who attend the oldest university in Cairo and the Moslem brotherhood who urge the Arabs to wage a holy war against Israel.
The Christian Century, in its editorial of January 20, 1954, challenged this inhuman exhortation in these terms:
This outburst sounded like the war cry of a savage, not the utterance of a responsible head of state. It should be rebuked and rebuked so effectively, that no more such wild counsel is heard from this, or similar sources.
In addition to this royal outburst the howl of a second, round has not been permitted by Egypt and other Arab states to subside for an instant.
Having only recently escaped from the greatest atrocities in history, the Israelis are horrified by the thought of further assaults. They are grateful to the United Nations for providing them a home after 2,000 years, and pray for the elementary human right to live in peace and security.
They cherish this little land, and it is only natural for them to resist to the last man, woman and child, any attempts to dislodge them from a single inch of it.
If they have to-and we pray to God that they will not have to-the Israelis will, as they did in 1948 and alone if necessary, again repel the war-crazed fanatics, fired by the cry of a holy war and nudged forward by a prowling and cunning bear.
The Israelis are not belligerent. They do not live by the sword and are religiously mindful of the remaining half of this prophetic admonition. They want to live in peace and they constantly proclaim their anxiety and willingness to negotiate a peace with the Arabs any time and anywhere. It is

the Arabs, on the other hand, who are intransigent, and even refuse to talk of peace.
The Israelis therefore are constantly kept on the defensive to preserve their little niche in the world, and, if they seek arms, they do so only to defensively meet the threats proclaimed daily by their surrounding neighbours. They are not in an arms race. If there is an arms race, let us recognize the mirage, since it is not between the Arabs and Israel, but is actually between communism and the democracies. That is far more menacing. Recognizing this danger quickly may preserve our Middle East position, hold intact the northern tier under the Baghdad pact, and prevent the whole continent of Africa from becoming communistic.
Can you therefore imagine, Mr. Speaker, my astonishment this afternoon when the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced an amendment in which he asked that all shipments of arms to the Middle East be arrested or stopped? I think that the hon. member for Prince Albert has placed himself in a most disturbing paradoxical position. At one moment he pleads in terms that the state of Israel must be kept secure and in the next moment introduces an amendment asking that the means of preserving the state should be removed from them. He asks that the state be preserved and promptly proceeds to tie their hands behind their backs by allowing arms to go to only one destination in the Middle East, and that is to Egypt. I did not think that was very noble or very brave of the hon. gentleman. I was shocked at the amendment and at the position now taken by the party to which the hon. member belongs. He states clearly to me, and I am sure to all my co-religionists, not only in this country but everywhere, that the little state of Israel should be left helpless and without arms to defend itself if it should be necessary.
Actually I was more surprised by his amendment when he dodged a reply to the question put to him by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I do not know why he refused to make a reply, but he turned around and asked, "What has the government done?" I would like to tell the hon. member what this government has done. This government has done more for the establishment and preservation of the state of Israel than any other country in the whole world.
We see the Soviet union's plans: its plans for Africa, its plans for the Middle East. We recognize them. All we have been doing in the past-we western nations-is to resort to a process of wooing, appeasing and perhaps praying. We are now obviously wooing the Arab nations by offering them arms and

money, all in the hope that we may be able to win them away from their crafty Soviet suitor. The armaments we pour into Egypt- when I say "we", I am talking now of all the western nations-all these armaments, peculiarly enough, appear to be going into a common arms pool with the communists. The great question, of course, is: Will the arms out of this common pool be used for us or against us? The Soviets can take the risk. They have nothing to lose. But can we take the risk? To find the answer to this sphinx-like question, we have merely to glance at contemporary history.
Do we forget that when Rommel was at El Alamein on his way to Alexandria, the Arabs were already rolling out the red carpet of welcome for him? Is our memory so short that we forget the Mufti's sojourn with Hitler? Do we forget so quickly that, in gratitude for Great Britain's help in building and maintaining the Suez canal, Egypt, at the very first opportunity, pressed for her dismissal? Do we forget the pro-Nazi revolt in Iraq led by Raschid-Ali during the early part of the second world war, which was greatly distressing to the allies? Do we forget that the Arab countries, all of them, remained comfortably neutral during two world wars when the democratic way of life was threatened? And have the Arabs throughout history earned the reputation that they can be trusted? Their record in that regard is not a creditable one. In fact, it dates back thousands of years to when the prophet Isaiah proclaimed an admonition against trust in Egypt, in the following words, and I quote chapter 36, verse six:
Lo, thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt, whereupon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it; so is Pharaoh King of Egypt to all that trust in him.
This is further supported by the fact that the Egyptians have now nudged Great Britain completely out of Egypt, notwithstanding the treaty condition that she will be readmitted in the event of apprehensive warfare, whatever that may mean. In my opinion, the United Kingdom will never voluntarily be readmitted to Egypt. Her departure was a cardinal blunder.
Disraeli foresaw the importance of the Suez canal and a strong British position in the Middle East. He gave that to the empire. He would now be writhing in anguish in his grave if he could see what has happened. From wherever Britain moved out, communism moved in. One shudders at the futility of a policy in the Middle East which lost for us links of empire and bastions of democracy, and reduced the stature of the 67509-47
External Affairs
United Kingdom in countries like India, Pakistan, the Suez, the Sudan, Cyprus and now Jordan. I am therefore astonished to find, even today, such an unrealistic approach to such painfully realistic problems.
Until the Egyptians disclosed Russia's tie-up with some Arab countries, the United Kingdom and the United States strained everything to hold Arab favour. This manoeuvring apparently called for the suppression of the real values in an alliance with Israel. These tactics may have been necessary, although I do not admit it, but now that the masks are off and we see the position and see where the Arabs are going, it is my respectful submission that to fail to make a show of strength and determination by including Israel in the western family would be a greater blunder than it was previously to suppress it. To proceed further by appeasement at this critical time is again unrealistic and a deplorable show of western weakness. It could well prove to be the blunder supreme that the west can make, and the appeasers may never be able to answer to destiny for their urging of it.
During the course of previous debates in this house, we have agreed that the most effective way to meet a Soviet challenge was by a show of strength and not by a show of weakness. Every time the west appeased- to use a colloquialism-we were taken for a ride, and we should by this time have learned our lesson.
If appeasement now is to take the form of attempting to throw the tiny state of Israel, or part of it, to the marauding Arabs, then I say it will not be as simple as some would have it, because the heroic people of Israel will not permit themselves to be Muniched into a Czechoslovakia. The irony of the situation is that appeasement will again have been resorted to in vain.
Let us recognize, even shamefacedly, that we are at this point, apart from a rebellious Cyprus, virtually left with the Baghdad pact alone and a prayer-if you will-that, despite the pressure exerted on some of its components, it will hold intact. If that, too, should not stand up-and it might not stand up-what remains? Virtually nothing, except Israel. This conclusion is being recognized more and more every day by western strategists.
Would it therefore not be most imprudent to miss the opportunity of availing ourselves of this additional safeguard? It is the only country in the Middle East that admittedly is western in every possible way and, because of that and its alliances with millions of brethren residing in western countries, Israel can be fully, completely and reliably depended upon. It has the best trained and

External Affairs
most disciplined army in the area and can yet prove to be our most reliable, trustworthy and able ally.
Let the. west fearlessly recognize this fact and declare to its allies of the Baghdad pact that it becomes urgent for the west to avail itself of Israel's position and strength, and emphasize that to do otherwise would definitely be shortsighted and dangerous, not only for the position of the west but also for the parties to the pact itself. Such a statement, Mr. Speaker, would tell the Arabs in no uncertain terms that we do not pussyfoot any longer in our determination to have peace in the Middle East. We must speak boldly and with firmness because until belligerent Arabs hear such a forthright declaration, made with grim determination, they are encouraged to gambit with stealthy and intriguing manoeuvres, including their threat to annihilate a million and a half people and, in their frenzy, launch a massacre that twentieth century civilization is anxious to live down. The western world must not remain silent any longer to this menacing talk lest it be considered an accessory to the fact resulting from its silence.
I would be loath Mr. Speaker to link this silence to the statement attributed to someone in Washington that Israel be written off as a noble experiment that failed. This is the sadistic utterance of an inhuman maniac, whoever he may be. No diplomatic manoeuvre, regardless of how great or important it may appear to be, could justify such premeditated and wholesale murder. It may suit the period of a Genghis Khan or an Attila but certainly not the enlightened and civilized twentieth century.
If Israel is an experiment that failed, then I say, Mr. Speaker, with horror and with shame, that the whole of our civilization is doomed to utter failure because I believe, that in the assessment by the Almighty of the actions and behaviour of men He recognizes values that are far more sacred and important than ruthless diplomatic expediencies.
I often wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether somewhere down the line the policy which the western powers have been following could not have been more skilful if it had been only a little more courageous and a little less influenced by vested interests.
The United Kingdom, the United States and France all have vested interests in the Middle East which they are anxious to preserve, and I believe that, in the very best of faith, then-assessment of the situation over the years may have been largely influenced by these interests, which could have coloured then-considerations as to the future and interfered
	' |
with their sober appreciation of wider horizons and the real human values.
Canada, on the other hand, which the world recognizes as the great arbiter and peace-seeking nation, has no direct or vested interests in that part of the world. Our diplomats enjoy the full confidence, respect and esteem of all the nations concerned and are therefore in the happy position of being able to see the situation objectively with open eyes and not through spectacles coloured or influenced by any vested or national interests. General Burns is already making a noble and valiant effort and would, no doubt, welcome support in his extremely difficult task.
It is, therefore, my submission, Mr. Speaker, that our country should, through its Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and his experts, promptly assess this complex mid-eastern situation and dauntlessly interject its good offices to help return to sanity those countries who stand on the brink of war and jeopardize the security of the entire world.
Careful study should be given to the fact that the vast majority of 50 million Arabs, because of their lack of education and miserable living conditions, are fertile for communist indoctrination. In all haste, therefore, the United Nations should provide substantial annual funds, either through a Marshall plan arrangement, through the Colombo plan or through any other international device, so that the standards of living of nomad Arab millions can be brought to some parallel with modern civilization. This will enable them to understand that the days of slavery are past, feudalism is archaic and that peace is the greatest gift human beings possess.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this might be a long process, whilst prompt action is necessary to arrest an impending conflagration. This, no doubt, partly explains the urgent conference between Sir Anthony Eden and President Eisenhower, as well as the hectic activities in Washington and London to woo Nasser away from communist enticements and thereby retain Arab support for the west. While I realize the importance of this, I also realize that it is even more important to Nasser himself. In the family of free nations he can retain for the Arabs their freedom and their independence but, as allies of Russia, they will become quickly submerged as satellites. Their leaders will become Russian puppets and their people, by an ironic quirk of history, may be exposed to the danger of possibly building twentieth century pyramids under the lash of communist taskmasters. I hope Colonel Nasser and his

advisers can see that far ahead and realize that the Arab nations are now themselves seriously at the crossroads.
We should, therefore, sincerely urge them to take a new look at their position and reconsider their relationship with their neighbours and the state of Israel in the light of the new dangers they themselves now face. They have, because of their persistent intransigence, already slipped into the communist quagmire from which they can, only with the co-operation of the west, still extricate themselves.
I am convinced that they are fully alert to their dangerous position but are crafty enough to still attempt to trade on our fears and our policy to appease. They must be made to know that this no longer exists. Consequently, now is the opportune time for the west to take an honourable and unwavering position.
We should tell Nasser bluntly: We want you on our side. We will help you retain your independence and guarantee your borders. We will help you financially in your program for economic and social reforms to raise the standard of living of your people. But we insist on having peace in the Middle East and you must stop this nonsense of threatening the annihilation of a state set up by the United Nations whose authority you must respect. We want you to know that we will never permit the action you threaten against Israel nor the creation of a second Egyptian bondage.
I would, Mr. Speaker, oppose with every ounce of my strength any form of approach that would say one word less. Under no circumstances must the free nations enter into a settlement based on fear, immoral diplomatic expediency, vested interests or appeasement of any type. That is the kind of quicksand on which our relations with the Arabs have unfortunately existed in the past. It has not only been weak and uncertain but it was historically and morally wrong. It has, moreover, proven to be a poor diplomatic assessment and has exploded in the faces of those who fostered it. Our so-called Middle East experts in London and Washington are now bewildered and running for cover. They should, therefore, alter their approach and completely abandon any form of appeasement or sacrifice if they seek a durable peace in the Middle East.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that in a sober assessment of the communist danger facing the Arab countries Colonel Nasser will realize that the advice of the free nations is honestly and sincerely given and is in the very best interests of all the Arab peoples. Contemporary history gives him good reason to 67509-474
External Affairs
appreciate the seriousness which motivates western statements because he no doubt remembers that, within the memory of this generation, the Arab people enjoyed great munificence, not from communism but from the free nations of the world. They liberated the Arabs from Turkish domination. They restored their kingdoms after the first world war. They provided them with western "know-how". They welcomed them into the family of nations and poured vast fortunes into their countries.
Moreover, it should also be emphasized that most of the Arab nations were established and recognized by international law and councils similar to the United Nations. If their own status as free and independent nations is to be respected, they must likewise respect the status of any other country established by the same authority.
The safeguarding of mutual rights and the maintenance of mutual respects are basic between free and democratic nations. With this guiding beacon in the hands of the United: Nations, I am hopeful that it can prevail upon Arab nations and the state of Israel, as urged last week by our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), to sit together at a round table to discuss a modus: vivendi.
I emphasize most solemnly and fervently, Mr. Speaker, that those who enter into peace negotiations with truth, good will and righteousness, will surely emerge from such a conference with justice, glory and dignity.

Mr. Speaker, during the time at my disposal this evening I intend to direct my remarks to the amendment and the subamendment which have been moved. As you will recall, the amendment was moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and it reads as follows:
That all the words alter "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
in view of the present critical situation in the Middle East, this house expresses its strong disapproval of the government's policy of authorizing the shipment of munitions of war to countries in that area not within the NATO alliance; and also condemns the government for the lack of candour with which the matter has been dealt with in this house.
Once again the opposition has to take the initiative. As reported at page 522 of Hansard the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated: ... X do not think it would be fair for me to consider that the debate in the house on that matter-
He was referring to the debate on the shipment of arms to the Middle East.
-has ended.

External Affairs
Despite that statement by the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) skilfully avoided touching upon the subject during his speech this afternoon. Had it not been originally for the questions which were asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) and by other members on this side of the house, I very much doubt whether the country would ever have heard of the shipment of these arms to Egypt and to Israel. The questions were raised by the opposition and I think that the members on this side of the house deserve credit for having brought this despicable dealing before the public eye at this time.
Reporters who first carried the story, after the question had been raised in this house, carried out their investigations and saw equipment being loaded at the Pugsley docks in the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, in the Egyptian freighter, Star of Assuan. They reported that aircraft and military vehicles were being loaded. In spite of the reported statements of government officials at the port of Saint John that this was only general cargo, the investigation was proceeded with. When questions were directly asked by myself in this house as to whether any equipment had been shipped over the weekend, the ministers had no knowledge of any equipment being sent. It was not until several days afterwards that the Secretary of State for External Affairs corroborated the reports. He corroborated those on January 24. Immediately following that speech by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) analysed it and described it as serving principally to expose the fumbling and floundering way in which the government has handled this issue since it arose in this house. Then he went on to say that the issue had been characterized by evasion, want of candour, ineptitude and incompetence or a mixture of all four.
Then again this afternoon the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) castigated the government for the way in which it had dealt with this situation. The question still remains: Why did it take the government so long to come clean and to make a clean breast of this extremely ugly situation? In fact, anything which has been said on the government side has only underlined the confusion and the incompetence of this ill-timed action. As has already been stated this afternoon, on January 10 an article appeared in the magazine Look over the name of
[Mr. Pearkes.l
the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In it is found this sentence:
In the Middle East war could flare up any day between Israel and the Arab states. The soviets are fanning the embers with arms shipments to Egypt.
I suggest that the ministers and the government have already added their little blow to fanning the embers of that possible conflagration which might break out there. It is against this background that we must analyse this shipment of arms to the Middle East. Against this background, when war might flare up at any moment, this government permitted the export of arms. It was certainly at a most ill-timed period. In fact, it was permitted at an extraordinarily dangerous time.
The shipments were first authorized last July. Ministerial approval was granted. During the last two or three weeks it has been extremely difficult to ascertain whether that approval was given by the cabinet, by three members of the cabinet or by one member of the cabinet himself. The description of the proceedings that was given this afternoon would make one think that perhaps only one member of the cabinet had any knowledge of the fact, although the Prime Minister stated that the cabinet accepted full responsibility for it. However, when this authorization was granted last July, although the conditions in the Middle East were extraordinarily unsettled, there was little indication that any war might be considered to be imminent. But this year, in this month when the shipments were allowed to leave this country, you can only say that conditions in the Middle East were inflamed and, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has already said, that war might flare up at any time.
During this period since July until now, the government did nothing about these shipments of arms. They realized that the situation in the Middle East was deteriorating. Did they tighten up their administration? Did they make inquiries into whether or not it was wise to send arms to this sensitive area, with the situation rapidly deteriorating? No, they just forgot that they had authorized the shipment of any arms at all. If it had not been for the questions which we on this side of the house asked I think that their forgetfulness would have been heartily welcomed by the government as a whole. There had been no check made. There had been no attempt to revise the export permits on equipment which was being sent from this country to the Middle East.
On January 25, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) gave a list of

the equipment which had been sent. There were three Harvard training aircraft to Egypt, the first of a consignment of 15 planes which had been authorized. These Harvard training planes were used and recognized as the best type of plane in which to train pilots for service aircraft. There were some spare parts as well as those three planes which were sent.
Then, Israel had been sent anti-tank equipment; 75 millimeter shells; tracks and spare parts for tanks. Let us remember that private traders were sending Valentine and Sherman tanks from England through France and Belgium to the Middle East. There were also 25-pounder field pieces such as the type we used during the second world war, and still a very effective weapon. There were machine guns, always convenient and handy for certain types of raiders and guerillas to carry. There were 3-7 anti-aircraft guns as well as some other items. The total came to over $2,800,000 during the last two years. You might say that those figures would not indicate there were any very large quantities of these weapons and ammunition sent. While the quantities sent have not been made available, it should be remembered that this equipment was considered by us to be obsolescent service equipment. One can well imagine, therefore, that this equipment was sold at bargain prices.
This equipment is considered by us to be obsolescent, that is not the type of equipment that our Canadian troops will require either for the defence of this country or to fulfil their NATO commitments in western Europe. We are thinking in terms of large numbers of troops equipped with modern arms, and what may be obsolescent to us may be considered a most effective weapon by other people who are not planning to have a force which would act as a deterrent to another world war. These machine guns, tanks and field artillery may be very effective weapons when used against tribesmen in the desert. Tracks and spare parts for tanks may be very useful in repairing tanks which have been shipped from elsewhere and which were demilitarized before the private traders sent them. It is bad enough for private traders to be trafficking in arms, but it is humiliating when we realize that our Canadian government has been trafficking in arms.
Some years ago this country was shocked by a series of articles which dealt with the arms trade as carried on by private manufacturers. They were entitled, "merchants of death". Is our government going to accept that title from now on if they are going to continue shipping arms? These articles on the
External Affairs
merchants of death showed quite clearly that there was plenty of evidence to prove that wars, particularly what may be described as minor wars, were fomented in order to increase the sale of arms. It would be farfetched to suggest that the government has any such thought, but we must remember that this government is selling our surplus equipment and taking money in return for lethal weapons which could be used against human beings. What is more despicable than anything else is that this government has stooped to sell to both sides in the dispute.
Of course the quantities have been limited and to date there is no question that the quantities which have been sent could upset the balance of arms in the Middle East. It is the principle of the government selling lethal weapons in a highly sensitive area and at a very critical time which is repugnant to me and I think repugnant to the majority of the people of Canada. The minister said it was not the policy to put a complete embargo on arms shipments except to the Sino-Soviet bloc and other countries, if any, where there was a threat to our own security. Well, from what point is that threat going to come? If war breaks out in the Middle East it is hardly likely that we, as a member of the United Nations, will be able to keep out of such a conflict. Why not put an embargo at this time on the shipment of arms to these sensitive areas? I have no quarrel about the shipment of arms to our allies in NATO or the other commonwealth countries. But why should we be shipping arms to every small country in sensitive areas?
We were told today that there were 34 such sensitive areas in the world today. It is all very well to utter pious statements that the shipments are not permitted to sensitive areas if they are of such a character that they might increase any temptation to commit aggression. But we are supplying machine guns, perhaps to trigger-happy tribesmen or nervous men on outpost duty who may very easily be tempted to commit an overt act.
It was only last December that a raid was carried out in Galilee. According to the United Nations report, no fewer than 41 Syrians were killed. Is it really necessary for us to inflame or fan these smouldering embers? When nations are facing each other and there is a possibility of war breaking out, it is not much use blaming them for getting arms from wherever they can. No; it is with the suppliers of those arms that the main responsibility rests.
At the present time we have no particular commitments with Israel any more than we have commitments with other Middle Eastern

External Affairs
powers. We have heard about the defensive grouping in the Middle East, which I believe was created by the United States, and that grouping includes Turkey, Iran, Pakistan and Iraq. Iraq, close to the borders of Israel, is regarded by Israel as being allied with the other Arab powers. One is not blaming Israel, and I do not blame Egypt. Egypt has become ;a leader of the Arab countries. And while Israel sees Egypt as the mainspring of the Arab efforts to prevent her survival, Egypt sees Israel as an intruder and potential aggressor brought into the area by the western powers. Egypt contends that it is Israel, with its large number of new settlers brought in from Europe, brought into a small and constricted area, that is responsible for the plight of 900,000 Arab refugees who have been forced to cross the border and who are today living in refugee camps in a degrading condition, both physically and morally. Israel is regarded not only as an intruder but also as a potential aggressor. As Israel's population grows, Egypt fears the new state will need more land, and where can Israel find it except just across her borders in Arab countries. She can find it only by expanding into her neighbour's territory, and so the argument runs.
If there is no war today, the Arab states must be ready to resist Israeli aggression tomorrow. And while Egypt talks of potential aggression by Israel, Egypt is suspected of aggressive motives by the Israelis. It is a tense and difficult situation, a situation which we should refuse to aggravate and, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has said, we should be most anxious to find a peaceful solution to this problem. Peaceful solutions have been offered. Did Mr. Dulles, in his address before the council of foreign relations last August, not offer a guarantee, to be sponsored by the United Nations, to both Israel and the Arab states against aggression, and did Sir Anthony Eden, in his speech before the Lord Mayor's banquet at the Guildhall, as reported in the magazine, Current History not do the same thing? These words are given as the exact text of his address:
Her Majesty's government and, I believe, the United States government and perhaps other powers too, would be prepared to give a formal guarantee to both sides; and that might bring real confidence and security at last. And our countries would also offer substantial help, financial and other, over this tragic problem of the refugees.
All this we will do.
Surely, that is a greater deterrent against the possibility of war breaking out between those two countries than supplying of arms to both of them, which can only be considered as creating a possibility of some sudden and overt act.

I should like to know what this government has done by way of offering a guarantee similar to that offered by the United States and by Great Britain. Are we prepared to play our part, not only by sending troops should war break out, but by letting it be known beforehand that if war does break out we will send troops? That is where the deterrent comes, having it clearly said beforehand what we will do. Has this government come out and stated what it will do? No. It forgets; it fumbles and it goes on shipping arms to both sides. I hope that this will not be considered as concluding the debate on the shipment of arms. I hope that before this debate is over the Secretary of State for External Affairs will renew the pledge which the Prime Minister gave, that for the time being no more arms will be shipped to either country, or to any area which is described as a sensitive area, unless that shipment takes place definitely to NATO, or commonwealth countries. Let us put an end to this trafficking in arms to countries which are non-NATO countries and countries which do not belong to our commonwealth. I repeat, I hope that before this debate is over the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or some other member of the government, will renew the pledge which was given the other day.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question before he finishes? I am very anxious to be clear about the last remark he addressed to the government? Did I understand him to advocate that there should be an embargo against all arms shipments by Canada to members, say, of the Baghdad pact, Iran, Iraq?
I said, to non-NATO and to non-commonwealth countries, and I will add any other country with which we have not a definite alliance.
Mr. Speaker, it is nearly ten o'clock; do you wish me to continue?
Go ahead.
Hurry up.
Proceed.

I rise to take part in this debate because this is an occasion when the life of a nation is at stake. Hon. members on the other side, members of the C.C.F. party, scoff at this suggestion. It is very easy for us to sit in this chamber where we are safe and secure and to be unaware of the danger in which a small country of a million and a half people are living under the shadow of the sword.

I want to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) upon the excellent statement of the government's policy in relation to the Middle East which he gave last Tuesday. Today we had the benefit of his statement of government policy in relation to other parts of the world. The clarity, comprehensiveness and balance of the statement indicates why the hon. member is held in such high esteem by people in all parts of the world.
I was shocked, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved an amendment in this manner. I want to read that amendment to the house:
That ... in view of the present critical situation in the Middle East, this house expresses its strong disapproval of the government's policy of authorizing the shipment of munitions of war to countries in that area not within the NATO alliance-
That is the part I want to deal with. I say I was shocked because it constituted a refusal of help to Israel in her hour of need. I never believed that the erstwhile great Conservative party would ever adopt a policy of that kind.
I was equally shocked by the amendment of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) because in principle his amendment affirmed the amendment made by the spokesman for the Conservative party. I say it did this in principle because the amendment was prospective and following the portion I read it added these words:
"without at the same time making sure that peace in that area would be guaranteed either by the United Nations or by the powers that signed the tripartite agreement of 1950, namely the United States, the United Kingdom and France."
It was obvious from the remarks of the hon. gentleman that what he was contemplating was the future shipment of arms because he did not want to bind the government's hands. He affirmed the amendment of the hon. member for Prince Albert that this house disapproved the shipment of arms to Israel.
Now what do the amendments mean in substance? The Secretary of State for External Affairs in his statement of a few days ago stated that in 1954 and in 1955 the total shipment of arms of this government to Israel amounted to $2,067,685.19 and to Egypt $771,121. That is the amount of arms shipped that is being disapproved of by the amendments laid before this house.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that while the amendment is limited to that small sum the whole question that is raised in this house at the present time is the shipment of arms to the Middle East and it is on that basis that I want to deal with the question.
External Affairs
It might be useful if I were to say a few words about the history of Israel. Hon. members will recall that the Balfour declaration was made December 2, 1917. It provided for the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people. Subsequently, after the termination of the first world war, a British mandate was set up on July 22, 1922, under the auspices of the league of nations and it was under the British mandate that Palestine carried on. In November 1947-I am not sure of these dates although I believe they are fairly accurate-the British government reached the decision that it would no longer carry on the mandate of Palestine and the United Nations resolved to set up the state of Israel under the partition agreement. I believe the partition was to take effect in the summer of 1948. It was in December 1947 that the incursion of the Arab bands began into Israel, the part that is occupied by the people who now constitute the Israeli people, and in the course of 1948 six Arab states took up arms against the people of Israel. There were Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon. That was a fight to the death for the people of Israel. They defended themselves in a way that won the admiration of all men in the free world. The result was that they forced Egypt and her allies to seek a truce and it was, I believe, in August 1949 that the armistice agreement was concluded. The result of what I have recounted to this point was that the state of Israel was established.
What has happened since 1949? Egypt has consistently refused to recognize Israel as a sovereign state. She would have no direct negotiations with Israel and any negotiations which occurred were conducted through a third party unless she was placed in circumstances such as the United Nations council when it was absolutely necessary for her to face Israel when she would have no other alternative.
The second major development to note during that period was that Egypt, through her ally Jordan, has consistently made attacks on the Israelis across the border into Israel. One need only take a look at the map to see what this means. It is a very easy matter for the Arabs, through Jordan, which crosses into Palestine and leaves a very narrow corridor, to make border attacks upon Israel, and since 1949 Egypt with her accomplices has continually made attacks upon the Israelis.
It is ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
For some time now, as a matter of fact ever since the conclusion of

External Affairs
the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I have wanted to present to the house a statement on the rule regarding the reading of speeches. I have not yet delivered that statement because the day following the conclusion of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne was the first private members' day. Friday was the first government day and I hesitated again on Monday to take any time from private members. We have now reached Tuesday and an important debate on external affairs is proceeding which is to be resumed tomorrow. I do not wish to delay the possibility of having hon. members look at the document and if it meets with the approval of hon. members I would ask their consent to have this text printed in the Votes and Proceedings. If I obtain the consent of hon. members to do this I will not read it tonight and hon. members will have an opportunity to look at it as soon as it is published. If they later wish to make
comments upon the statement I would imagine that arrangements could be made to that end through the usual channels.
May I point out that this statement recites the rule as established by the authorities on procedure and also the practice of this house under it. Suggestions are made. I do not contend for one moment that the suggestions that are herein contained will produce a cure-all as far as the reading of speeches is concerned, but I hope that these suggestions will be received in the spirit in which they have been prepared, namely, with the object of the improvement of our debate and thus for the good of parliament.
If it meets with the approval of hon. members, I would suggest that the text be printed in Votes and Proceedings. Is it agreed?
Agreed.
It being two minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
